sections.s5_journey:
Input data: SAV2001 at 1000000, CUR3001 at 250000; each operation called twice to simulate a retry.

Step 1: GET balance is called twice. Both reads return the same balance and the server state is untouched, confirming GET is idempotent and safe for intermediaries to retry.

Step 2: PUT address is called twice with the same address. The first call sets the address; the second overwrites it with the identical value, so the stored address is the same after one or two calls. PUT replaces, so it is idempotent.

Step 3: DELETE standing-instruction is called twice. The first removes it; the second finds nothing to remove and leaves it absent. The end state, absent, is the same after one or many calls, so DELETE is idempotent.

Step 4: The naive transfer POST is called twice without a key. The first moves 50000, taking CUR3001 to 300000; the retry moves another 50000, taking it to 350000. The non-idempotent POST double-applied, which in production would be a double charge.

Step 5: The keyed transfer POST is called twice with key K-1. The first moves 20000 and stores the result under K-1. The retry finds K-1 already stored and returns the saved result without moving money again, so CUR3001 increases by exactly 20000. The idempotency key made the POST safe.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Idempotency means that performing the same operation many times leaves the system in the same state as performing it exactly once; repeated identical requests do not change state beyond the first application. The subtlety I always point out is that this is about the resulting state, not about the response being byte-identical, so a second DELETE returning 404 instead of 204 is still idempotent because the resource is equally gone either way.

On the HTTP methods, GET and HEAD are safe and idempotent because they only read. PUT is idempotent because it replaces a resource with a given representation, so repeating it sets the same value. DELETE is idempotent because deleting an already-deleted resource leaves it deleted. OPTIONS is idempotent because it only describes capabilities. POST is not idempotent because it creates a new resource or runs a command, so two identical POSTs usually do the thing twice, and PATCH is not inherently idempotent because a relative update like incrementing a balance changes state on every call.

Why it matters is that the network is unreliable at every layer, so clients time out and retry, mobile apps on flaky connections resend, and load balancers and proxies are actually allowed to automatically retry idempotent methods on connection failure. If the operation is idempotent all of those retries are harmless, but if it is not, a retry can double-charge a customer, create a duplicate loan application, or post interest twice. The method semantics are a contract that intermediaries rely on, which is why hiding a money-moving side effect behind a GET is a serious bug. The hard reality is that payments and transfers are fundamentally POST operations, which are not idempotent by definition, yet they are exactly where a duplicate hurts most, so I close that gap with an idempotency key: the client sends a unique key per logical operation, the server stores the key with the first result, and a retry carrying the same key returns the stored result instead of acting again, which is how payment APIs like Stripe make POST safe.

On my project at National Bank of India this showed up concretely. A profile-address update was modeled as a POST that appended, so a retry created a duplicate address, and we fixed it by making it a PUT that replaces, which is naturally idempotent. A GET had been wired through a bug to recompute and persist interest, and a load balancer retry posted interest twice, which taught the team that reads must be pure. And because transfers are unavoidably POST, we added an Idempotency-Key header backed by a Redis store so a retried transfer returns the original result instead of moving money again.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that idempotency means repeating a request yields the same end state as doing it once, GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, and OPTIONS are idempotent while POST and PATCH are not, and it matters because unreliable networks cause retries at every layer, so I model true updates as PUT, keep reads side-effect-free, and protect non-idempotent commands like payments with an idempotency key.

answers.shortTitle: What are the different ways to implement idempotency and when do you use each

s1_definition.profdef: There are four main techniques for implementing idempotency. Idempotency keys store a client-supplied key mapped to the first response and replay that response on retry, which is ideal for payments. Database unique constraints let the database reject duplicate records atomically, which is ideal for preventing duplicate inserts. State-based validation skips the operation if the resource is already in the target state, which is ideal for transitions. Distributed locks serialize access so only one operation wins, which is ideal for one-time resources under high concurrency. You pick the technique based on whether you are replaying a response, preventing a duplicate row, enforcing a state transition, or guarding a single scarce resource.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India there are four ways the staff avoid doing something twice. The idempotency key is like giving Rajesh a receipt number so if he asks again they just hand back the same receipt instead of redoing the payment. The unique constraint is like the ledger physically refusing a second entry with the same cheque number. State-based validation is like the clerk seeing the account is already closed and not closing it again. The distributed lock is like a single festival coupon counter where only one teller at a time can hand out the last coupon so it is never given twice.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use idempotency keys to replay a stored payment response, unique constraints to block duplicate rows, state checks to skip already-done transitions, and distributed locks to guard a single scarce resource under concurrency.

sections.s2_technical:
The idempotency key technique is the right tool when a client command may be retried and you must return the same outcome, classically payments. The client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it, typically in an `Idempotency-Key` header. The server, on the first request, performs the operation and stores a mapping from the key to the full response, including status and body. On a retry with the same key, the server detects the key already exists and returns the stored response without re-running the operation. For example `if (store.containsKey(key)) return store.get(key); else { var resp = charge(); store.put(key, resp); return resp; }`. The subtlety is concurrency: two requests with the same key may arrive simultaneously, so the store-and-check must be atomic, usually a unique insert of the key or a lock, and you must handle the in-progress case so the second caller waits or gets a conflict rather than double-charging.

Database unique constraints are the right tool when the goal is to prevent duplicate records and the database can enforce it atomically. You add a unique index on a natural business key, for example a unique constraint on `transaction_reference`, and let the insert fail with a duplicate-key error on the second attempt. For example `INSERT INTO payments(reference, ...) VALUES(?, ...)` with `UNIQUE(reference)` throws on the duplicate, and you catch that as "already processed" rather than an error. This is extremely robust because the guarantee lives in the database and survives application crashes and race conditions, and it requires no extra lookup because the constraint does the work.

State-based validation is the right tool when the operation is a state transition and repeating it is a no-op if the resource is already in the target state. Before acting you check the current state and skip if it is already there. For example cancelling an order: `if (order.getStatus() == CANCELLED) return; else order.cancel();`. This naturally makes the operation idempotent without any extra storage, and it is the cleanest option when the domain already has a clear state machine. The caution is that the check-and-act must be atomic under concurrency, which you get with optimistic locking via a version column or a conditional update like `UPDATE orders SET status='CANCELLED' WHERE id=? AND status<>'CANCELLED'` that affects zero rows on the second call.

Distributed locks are the right tool when a single scarce resource must be handed out exactly once under high concurrency across many instances, such as a one-time coupon, the last ticket, or the last unit of stock. You acquire a lock, typically in Redis with `SET key value NX PX ttl`, do the critical operation, and release it, so only one request wins. For example only the holder of the lock on `coupon:DIWALI50` may redeem it. This is heavier than the other options and should be used only when the resource is genuinely single-winner, because locks add latency and failure modes like lock expiry. A senior nuance is that you prefer the cheaper techniques first: a unique constraint or a conditional update often gives you the same single-winner guarantee as a distributed lock without the lock's operational cost, so you reach for a distributed lock only when the contended resource is not naturally a database row you can constrain. The techniques also compose: a payment endpoint often uses an idempotency key at the edge and a unique constraint on the transaction reference in the database as a second line of defense.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Rajesh's payment request can be retried by his phone, and the bank must return the original result rather than charge again. This is exactly the idempotency-key technique, storing the key to the response and replaying it.

Problem 2 — A batch loader occasionally receives the same transaction reference twice and must not create two ledger rows. This is exactly the unique-constraint technique, letting the database reject the duplicate atomically.

Problem 3 — A "close account" command may be clicked twice, and closing an already-closed account should do nothing. This is exactly the state-based technique, skipping if the status is already CLOSED.

Problem 4 — A festival campaign gives one 50-rupee coupon per customer, and under a traffic spike two concurrent requests must not both redeem it. This is exactly the distributed-lock technique, serializing redemption so only one wins.

Our mini-project demonstrates all four. The code defines a `PaymentService` using an idempotency key, a `LedgerLoader` using a unique-reference set to reject duplicates, an `AccountService` using state-based validation to close accounts, and a `CouponService` using a lock to redeem a one-time coupon under concurrent access, plus a demo that exercises each technique with a duplicate attempt.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a payment with key K-PAY-1 submitted twice; ledger reference TXN-9 inserted twice; account SAV2001 closed twice; coupon DIWALI50 redeemed by two concurrent requests.

Step 1: The payment service receives K-PAY-1, finds no stored response, charges 50000, generates a transaction id, and stores the response under the key. The retry with K-PAY-1 finds the stored response and returns it unchanged, so the charge happened once.

Step 2: The ledger loader inserts TXN-9, which succeeds because the reference is new. The second insert of TXN-9 is rejected by the unique set exactly as a database unique constraint would reject it, preventing a duplicate row.

Step 3: The account service closes SAV2001, transitioning it to CLOSED. The second close sees the account is already CLOSED and performs a no-op, so the transition is idempotent.

Step 4: Two threads concurrently try to redeem coupon DIWALI50. They contend on the lock; the winner records the redemption and returns REDEEMED, while the loser, after the lock is released, sees the coupon already redeemed and returns ALREADY REDEEMED. The one-time coupon was handed out exactly once.

Step 5: The combined output shows each technique preventing a double effect in the way best suited to its scenario.

sections.s6_takeaway:
There are four main ways to implement idempotency, and the skill is matching the technique to the scenario rather than reaching for one tool every time. The idempotency key stores a client-supplied key mapped to the first response and replays that response on retry, which is the right choice for payments where the client may retry and must get the original outcome rather than a second charge. The database unique constraint lets the database reject a duplicate record atomically, which is the right choice for preventing duplicate inserts like a repeated transaction reference. State-based validation skips the operation if the resource is already in the target state, which is the right choice for transitions like closing an account. And a distributed lock serializes access so only one operation wins, which is the right choice for a single scarce resource under high concurrency, like a one-time coupon or the last ticket.

For the idempotency key I store the key to the full response on the first call and, on a retry carrying the same key, return the stored response without re-running the operation. The subtlety I always mention is concurrency: two requests with the same key can arrive together, so the store-and-check has to be atomic, usually a unique insert of the key, and I handle the in-progress case so the second caller waits or gets a conflict rather than double-charging. For the unique constraint I add a unique index on the natural business key and treat the duplicate-key error as already-processed, which is wonderfully robust because the guarantee lives in the database and survives crashes and races.

For state-based validation I check the current state and skip if it is already the target, which needs no extra storage and is cleanest when the domain already has a state machine, but the check-and-act must be atomic, so I use a conditional update like setting status to CLOSED only where the status is not already CLOSED, which affects zero rows on the second call. For the distributed lock I acquire a Redis lock with SET NX and a TTL, do the critical work, and release, so only one request handles the scarce resource. The senior point I make is that I prefer the cheaper techniques first, because a unique constraint or a conditional update often gives the same single-winner guarantee as a distributed lock without the lock's latency and expiry failure modes, so I use a distributed lock only when the contended resource is not naturally a database row I can constrain.

On my project at National Bank of India we used all four. Payments carried an Idempotency-Key backed by Redis so a retried charge replayed the stored response. The batch ledger loader relied on a unique constraint on the transaction reference so a repeated file never created duplicate rows. The close-account command used a conditional state transition so a double click was a no-op. And a festival one-coupon-per-customer campaign used a Redis lock so two concurrent redemptions could not both succeed. We also composed them, putting an idempotency key at the payment edge and a unique constraint on the transaction reference in the database as a second line of defense.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I implement idempotency with an idempotency key to replay a stored payment response, a unique constraint to block duplicate rows, a state check to skip already-done transitions, and a distributed lock to guard a single scarce resource, and I pick the technique by the scenario while preferring database-enforced guards over locks wherever possible.

Retries from the client or the payment provider are handled by returning the stored result for a known key rather than performing the charge again.

The ledger also physically refuses two entries with the same ticket number, so even if two clerks act at the same instant, only one entry can exist.

sections.s2_technical:
First understand the race. Two requests for the same logical payment arrive almost simultaneously, perhaps the client timed out and retried while the first was still in flight, or the payment provider retried its webhook. Both check "has this payment been processed?", both see no, and both proceed to charge. The window between the check and the write is where the race lives, so the fix must make the check-and-claim atomic and must have a hard backstop even if the application logic races.

The outermost layer is the idempotency key per request. The client generates a unique key for the logical payment and sends it on every attempt including retries. The server uses this key as the identity of the operation. The critical implementation detail is that claiming the key must be atomic: you do not read-then-write in two steps, you attempt a single atomic insert of the key with an in-progress status. If the insert succeeds you are the first and you proceed; if it fails with a duplicate-key error, someone else owns this operation, so you either return their stored result or, if they are still in progress, wait or return a conflict. This single atomic claim closes the check-then-act window.

The hard backstop is a unique database constraint on the transaction id or payment reference. Even if two threads somehow both believe they are first, the database will allow only one row with that transaction id; the second insert fails atomically. This is the guarantee you can actually trust under concurrency because it is enforced by the database, not by hopeful application code. You catch the duplicate-key exception and treat it as "already processed", then return the existing result.

Transaction management ties it together. The charge, the ledger update, and the idempotency or transaction record must commit in the same database transaction, so you can never end up with money moved but no record, or a record but no money. If the transaction rolls back, both disappear and the client can safely retry. Atomic operations like a conditional update, for example `UPDATE payments SET status='DONE' WHERE id=? AND status='PENDING'`, give you single-winner semantics inside the database without a separate lock.

A distributed lock is used only where truly needed, which is when the contended resource is not a database row you can constrain, for example a one-time external coupon or a rate-limited external gateway slot. For an ordinary payment keyed by transaction id, a unique constraint is cheaper and safer than a distributed lock, so you do not reach for a lock by default.

Finally, handling retries so a retry returns the original result. Once the first request completes, you store the full response, status and body, against the idempotency key. Any subsequent request with the same key, whether from the client, a proxy, or the payment provider, is detected and the stored response is returned verbatim without charging again. The senior nuances are: give idempotency records a TTL appropriate to the retry window; handle the in-progress case explicitly so a retry arriving before the first finishes does not double-charge, typically by making the second caller wait on the row lock or return 409 so the client retries later; make the key scope correct so it identifies the logical operation, not the HTTP attempt; and remember the same discipline applies to asynchronous consumers, where at-least-once delivery is just another source of retries that a processed-id check must absorb.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Rajesh's app timed out mid-payment and retried while the first request was still processing, and both requests charged him, so he paid twice. This is exactly why the idempotency-key claim must be a single atomic insert, so the second request cannot also believe it is first.

Problem 2 — Even with the key check, a true thread race slipped two charges through once. This is exactly why we add a unique constraint on the transaction id as a hard database backstop that only one row can satisfy.

Problem 3 — The payment provider retried its confirmation webhook, and the system must return the original result rather than re-charge. This is exactly why we store the response against the key and replay it on any retry.

Our mini-project builds a payment service hardened against the race. The code defines a `PaymentRequest` with an idempotency key, a `PaymentStore` that atomically claims a key and enforces a unique transaction id, a `PaymentService` that charges inside a transaction-like critical section and stores the response, and a demo that fires two concurrent requests with the same key to prove only one charge happens, then simulates a provider retry that returns the stored result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one logical payment with idempotency key IDEM-RAJESH-77 and transaction id TXN-77, fired by two concurrent threads, then retried once by the provider.

Step 1: Both threads are released at the same instant and both call `claimKey("IDEM-RAJESH-77")`. Because the claim is an atomic put-if-absent, exactly one thread gets true and the other gets false. The race is resolved at the claim, not at a separate check.

Step 2: The winning thread inserts the unique transaction id TXN-77, which succeeds, then records the charge, builds the response, and completes the key by storing the response and marking it DONE.

Step 3: The losing thread, having failed the claim, sees the key is in progress, waits briefly until it becomes DONE, and then returns the stored response. It never charges.

Step 4: The charge counter shows exactly one, proving that despite two concurrent requests only one charge was applied.

Step 5: The payment provider retries the same request later. The claim fails because the key exists and is DONE, so the service immediately replays the stored response without charging, and the counter stays at one.

```
2026-10-24 14:17:40 INFO    Performed charge for TXN-77
2026-10-24 14:17:40 INFO    RACE result A = CHARGED SAV2001 Rs.50000 txn=TXN-77
2026-10-24 14:17:40 INFO    RACE result B = CHARGED SAV2001 Rs.50000 txn=TXN-77 (replayed after wait)
2026-10-24 14:17:40 INFO    Total charges applied for TXN-77 = 1
2026-10-24 14:17:40 INFO    PROVIDER retry = CHARGED SAV2001 Rs.50000 txn=TXN-77 (replayed stored result)
2026-10-24 14:17:40 INFO    Total charges after provider retry = 1
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The first thing I do with this scenario is name the race precisely: two requests for the same logical payment arrive almost simultaneously, often because the client timed out and retried while the first was still in flight or the payment provider retried its webhook, both check whether the payment was processed, both see no, and both charge. The window between that check and the write is where the double charge is born, so my whole design is about collapsing that window and adding a hard backstop that holds even if the application logic races.

The outermost defense is an idempotency key per request that the client sends on every attempt including retries, and the crucial implementation detail is that claiming the key must be a single atomic operation, not a read-then-write. I attempt one atomic insert of the key; if it succeeds I am the first and I proceed, and if it fails as a duplicate, someone else owns the operation, so I either replay their stored result or, if they are still in progress, wait on the row or return a conflict. The hard backstop beneath that is a unique database constraint on the transaction id, because even if two threads somehow both think they are first, the database allows only one row with that transaction id and the second insert fails atomically. That database-enforced guarantee is the one I actually trust under concurrency, not hopeful application code.

I bind these together with transaction management, committing the charge, the ledger update, and the idempotency or transaction record in the same transaction so I can never end up with money moved but no record or a record with no money, and if it rolls back both vanish and the client can safely retry. I use atomic conditional updates for single-winner semantics inside the database, and I reach for a distributed lock only where the contended resource is not a database row I can constrain, like a one-time external coupon, because for an ordinary payment a unique constraint is cheaper and safer than a lock. Then the retry handling falls out naturally: once the first request completes I store the full response against the key, and any later request with the same key, from the client, a proxy, or the provider, is detected and the stored response is replayed verbatim without charging again.

On my project at National Bank of India this came from a real incident where Rajesh's app retried mid-payment and he was charged twice, and later a genuine thread race slipped two charges through. We hardened the flow with an atomic idempotency-key claim as an insert, a unique constraint on the transaction id as the database backstop, the charge and the record committed in one transaction, and the full response stored against the key so provider webhook retries replay the original result. The explicit in-progress handling, where a second concurrent request waits or gets a 409 rather than double-charging, was the detail that finally made the concurrent case safe.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I prevent a double charge end to end with an atomic idempotency-key claim, a unique constraint on the transaction id as the hard database backstop, and a single transaction that commits the charge and the record together, so every client or provider retry returns the stored result instead of charging again, and I only add a distributed lock when the scarce resource is not a row I can constrain.

---

answers.question: (Scenario) What happens if the application crashes AFTER a payment succeeds but BEFORE the response reaches the client (the client retries, risking a double charge), and why does this make server-side idempotency — not client discipline — the only safe design?
answers.shortTitle: (Scenario) What happens if the application crashes AFTER a payment succeeds but BEFORE the response reaches the client

s1_definition.profdef: If the server commits a payment and then crashes before the response reaches the client, the client sees only a timeout or connection error and cannot tell whether the charge succeeded or failed, so a well-behaved client retries, and that retry risks a second charge. Because the client genuinely cannot distinguish a lost success from a real failure, correctness cannot depend on client behavior; it must be guaranteed on the server with idempotency keyed to the logical operation, so that a retry of a request that already succeeded returns the original result instead of charging again.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh hands the teller a payment slip, the teller processes it and the money moves, but before the teller can hand back the receipt the power cuts out and Rajesh is sent home. Rajesh has no idea whether his payment went through, so he comes back the next day and submits the slip again. If the bank relied on Rajesh to "just not resubmit", it would be relying on something he cannot possibly know. Only the bank, by recognizing the slip's unique number and seeing it was already processed, can safely hand back the original receipt instead of charging him twice.
s1_definition.oneliner: A crash after commit but before the response is indistinguishable from a failure to the client, so the client must retry, and only server-side idempotency keyed to the operation can make that retry safe, never client discipline.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** If the server commits a payment and then crashes before the response reaches the client, the client sees only a timeout or connection error and cannot tell whether the charge succeeded or failed, so a well-behaved client retries, and that retry risks a second charge. Because the client genuinely cannot distinguish a lost success from a real failure, correctness cannot depend on client behavior; it must be guaranteed on the server with idempotency keyed to the logical operation, so that a retry of a request that already succeeded returns the original result instead of charging again.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh hands the teller a payment slip, the teller processes it and the money moves, but before the teller can hand back the receipt the power cuts out and Rajesh is sent home. Rajesh has no idea whether his payment went through, so he comes back the next day and submits the slip again. If the bank relied on Rajesh to "just not resubmit", it would be relying on something he cannot possibly know. Only the bank, by recognizing the slip's unique number and seeing it was already processed, can safely hand back the original receipt instead of charging him twice.

**One line to remember:** A crash after commit but before the response is indistinguishable from a failure to the client, so the client must retry, and only server-side idempotency keyed to the operation can make that retry safe, never client discipline.

sections.s2_technical:
Trace the exact sequence. The request arrives, the server validates it, performs the charge, and commits the transaction, so the money has definitively moved and the database reflects it. Then, before the HTTP response is written back, the process crashes, or the network drops, or a load balancer times out. From the client's side all it observes is that the connection failed or timed out. Here is the core problem: a lost-success and a genuine-failure look absolutely identical to the client. There is no information in a timeout that says "but actually it worked". The client cannot inspect the server's database.

Given that ambiguity, what should a correct client do? It should retry, because if the request actually failed, not retrying would silently drop a payment the user intended, which is also unacceptable. So retrying is the right client behavior, and retrying is exactly what creates the double-charge risk. This is why you cannot solve the problem by telling clients "do not retry" or "retry carefully": the client lacks the information to make that decision correctly, so any rule you give it is either unsafe, retry and risk double charge, or also unsafe, do not retry and risk lost payment.

Because client discipline cannot be correct in principle, the guarantee must live on the server. The mechanism is idempotency keyed to the logical operation. The client attaches a stable idempotency key that is the same across the original request and all its retries, representing the single logical payment. On the first request the server performs the charge and, in the same transaction that commits the charge, records the key together with the response. On a retry carrying that same key, the server finds the committed record and returns the stored result without charging again. The reason this survives the crash is that the key record and the charge commit atomically: if the charge committed, the key record committed too, so the retry is guaranteed to find it and replay rather than re-charge.

Several senior points make this robust against the crash specifically. The idempotency record and the business change must be in one transaction; if you wrote the key in a separate step, a crash between them would leave a charge with no key and the retry would double-charge, which is the dual-write problem. You must handle the in-progress case, because the crash could happen while the first request was mid-flight and the retry arrives before any record exists at all; here the unique constraint on the key or transaction id is the backstop that lets only one of them win. The idempotency key must be chosen by the client before the first attempt and reused on retries, not generated per HTTP call, otherwise retries look like new operations. And the response must be durably stored, not just the fact of success, so the retry can return the exact original result the client expected. The same reasoning extends to asynchronous processing: a consumer that commits then crashes before acknowledging will see the message redelivered, which is the messaging twin of this scenario and is solved the same way, with an idempotent, durably-recorded processed id.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The payment service charged Rajesh and committed, then the pod was killed by an autoscaler before the response was sent, so Rajesh's app timed out and retried. This is exactly the lost-success scenario, and only a durable idempotency record committed with the charge lets the retry replay the original result.

Problem 2 — Early on, the team wrote the idempotency key in a second step after the charge, and a crash between them caused a double charge. This is exactly why the key and the charge must commit in a single transaction.

Problem 3 — The crash sometimes happened before any record existed, so two requests raced with no prior record. This is exactly why a unique constraint on the key is the backstop that lets only one win.

Our mini-project simulates the crash. The code defines a `PaymentService` whose `pay` commits the charge and the idempotency record atomically, a `CrashablePaymentService` wrapper that commits then throws before returning to mimic the crash, and a demo that performs a payment that "crashes" after commit, then retries with the same key and shows the stored result is replayed with no second charge, contrasted with a broken version that wrote the key separately.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a payment with key IDEM-RAJESH-88 and transaction TXN-88 that commits then crashes, followed by a client retry with the same key; plus a broken path for contrast.

Step 1: The safe service charges Rajesh and records the key, transaction id, and response all in one atomic unit, so the charge and the idempotency record commit together. The charge count is now one.

Step 2: Immediately after the commit the process throws a simulated crash before any response is returned. The client sees only a failure and has no way to know the charge actually succeeded.

Step 3: The client, unable to distinguish success from failure, retries with the same key IDEM-RAJESH-88. The safe service finds the stored response committed in step one and replays it without charging again. The charge count stays at one.

Step 4: For contrast, the broken service charges and commits but writes the key in a separate step, then crashes before that write. The key was never recorded.

Step 5: The broken retry finds no key, believes this is a new operation, and charges again, producing a double charge. This demonstrates concretely why the key and the charge must commit atomically and why client discipline could not have saved it.

```

2026-10-24 14:19:05 INFO    After crash: charges for TXN-88 = 1
2026-10-24 14:19:05 INFO    Client retry (same key) → CHARGED SAV2001 Rs.50000 txn=TXN-88 (replayed stored result)
2026-10-24 14:19:05 INFO    SAFE total charges = 1
2026-10-24 14:19:05 WARNING BROKEN crash between charge and key write
2026-10-24 14:19:05 SEVERE  BROKEN total charges = 2 (DOUBLE CHARGE)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
I start by tracing the exact sequence, because the whole answer hinges on it. The server validates the request, performs the charge, and commits, so the money has definitively moved. Then, before the response is written back, the process crashes or the network drops. There is nothing in a timeout that reveals the charge actually went through, and the client cannot inspect the server's database.

Given that ambiguity, the correct client behavior is to retry, because if the request really did fail, not retrying would silently drop a payment the user intended, which is just as unacceptable as a double charge. So retrying is right, and retrying is exactly what creates the double-charge risk. That is the heart of why client discipline cannot be the solution: any rule I give the client is unsafe in one direction or the other, because the client lacks the information needed to decide correctly. Telling clients not to retry risks lost payments, and telling them to retry risks double charges.

Because correctness cannot depend on something the client cannot know, the guarantee has to live on the server, and the mechanism is idempotency keyed to the logical operation. The client attaches a stable key that is the same across the original request and every retry, the server performs the charge and records that key together with the response in the same transaction, and a retry carrying the same key finds the committed record and replays the stored result instead of charging again. The reason this survives the crash is atomicity: if the charge committed, the key record committed with it, so the retry is guaranteed to find it. The classic mistake, which I have seen cause real double charges, is writing the key in a separate step after the charge, because a crash in between leaves a charge with no key and the retry charges again, which is just the dual-write problem.

On my project at National Bank of India this was not hypothetical: an autoscaler killed a payment pod right after the charge committed but before the response was sent, Rajesh's app timed out and retried, and because we committed the idempotency key and the response in the same transaction as the charge, the retry simply replayed the original receipt and no second charge occurred. We also kept a unique constraint on the key and transaction id as a backstop for the case where the crash happened before any record existed and two requests raced. The lesson I draw is blunt: the network and the process are both unreliable, the client can never tell a lost success from a failure, so server-side atomic idempotency is the only design that is correct, and client politeness is never a substitute for it.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that a crash after commit but before the response is indistinguishable from a failure, so the client must retry, which means only server-side idempotency, with the key and the charge committed atomically, can make that retry replay the original result rather than charge again, and that is why correctness lives on the server and never in client discipline.

sections.s2_technical:
The danger is a mismatch between what the user believes and what is actually true in the system of record. A payment is not real until the transaction that moves money and records it has durably committed. Before that commit, many things can still make it fail: the account turns out to have insufficient funds, a unique or foreign-key constraint is violated, a fraud check rejects it at the last moment, the database connection drops, or the process crashes mid-commit and the transaction rolls back. If you showed "confirmed" before the commit and then the commit fails, you have told the user a payment happened when it did not. The user may ship goods, stop worrying about a bill, or make decisions based on a false confirmation, and now you have a support and reconciliation problem that is far worse than an honest "pending".

There is also a deeper correctness point about optimistic UI. It is tempting to argue "the commit almost always succeeds, so show confirmed and only correct it on the rare failure", but in payments the cost of a false positive is severe and asymmetric: a wrongly-shown confirmation can lead to real-world actions that are hard to reverse, whereas a slightly slower honest confirmation costs only a little latency. For money, correctness of the message must dominate perceived snappiness.

The correct design is to drive the user-facing message from the real committed outcome. For a fast synchronous payment, the flow is: accept the request, perform the charge, wait for the database commit to return success, and only then respond with "confirmed". If the commit fails or rolls back, you respond with a clear failure or an error the user can act on. The confirmation and the commit are causally linked, so the UI never shows something the system does not durably believe.

For long-running work, where the payment involves slow steps like external gateway calls, SWIFT, or multi-service orchestration, you do not hold the UI hostage to a confirmation that may take seconds or minutes. Instead you return 202 Accepted immediately with a pending or processing state and a handle, for example a status URL or a job id. The client then either polls that status endpoint or receives a push notification or webhook when the work completes. Crucially, the status transitions from PENDING to CONFIRMED only when the durable commit of the final step has actually happened, and to FAILED if it did not. So even in the asynchronous case the confirmation is still driven by the real committed outcome; you have simply decoupled the acknowledgment of receipt from the confirmation of success.

Several senior nuances complete the picture. The pending state must be explicit in the UI so the user understands the payment is not yet final and does not take irreversible action prematurely. The status store must be durable so that a crash does not lose the pending job. The transition to CONFIRMED should be idempotent and derived from the committed record, not from an in-memory flag, so a replay or a duplicate notification cannot flip a failed payment to confirmed. And you should still send the user a definitive notification on completion so they are not left polling forever. This pending-then-confirmed model is also exactly how you reconcile with external providers whose final answer arrives asynchronously via webhook.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A product manager at National Bank of India asked to show "payment confirmed" the instant Rajesh tapped pay, to make the app feel fast, but some of those payments later failed the final fraud commit and rolled back, leaving customers believing they had paid. This is exactly why the confirmation must be driven by the durable committed outcome, not an optimistic guess.

Problem 2 — For international transfers that take seconds on SWIFT, holding the UI until commit felt sluggish. This is exactly why we return 202 with a PENDING state and let the client poll or be notified, so the app stays responsive without lying.

Problem 3 — A duplicate webhook once tried to flip a FAILED payment to CONFIRMED. This is exactly why the final status must be derived idempotently from the committed record.

Our mini-project builds a payment confirmation flow. The code defines a `Payment` with a status lifecycle, a `PaymentService` whose synchronous path confirms only after a commit that may fail, and whose long-running path returns PENDING and later transitions based on the committed outcome, a `StatusStore`, and a demo that shows a successful confirm-after-commit, a failed commit that correctly shows FAILED rather than a false confirmed, and a long-running payment that goes PENDING then CONFIRMED on the real outcome.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: PAY-1 fast payment that commits, PAY-2 fast payment whose commit fails, PAY-3 long-running payment.

Step 1: PAY-1 starts as PENDING, the service attempts the durable commit, which succeeds, and only then transitions the status to CONFIRMED. The UI message "confirmed" is now truthful because it follows the real commit.

Step 2: PAY-2 starts as PENDING, the service attempts the commit, which rolls back due to a last-minute fraud or funds failure, and the status becomes FAILED. The UI shows an honest failure and the money was never charged, so the user is not misled.

Step 3: PAY-3 is long-running, so the service immediately returns 202 Accepted with a PENDING status and a status URL. The UI shows "processing", not "confirmed", so the user does not take irreversible action yet.

Step 4: A background worker performs the slow SWIFT work and attempts the durable commit, which succeeds, then transitions PAY-3 to CONFIRMED based on that real committed outcome. The transition is idempotent and would never flip a FAILED payment to CONFIRMED.

Step 5: The client polls the status URL and sees PENDING on early polls and CONFIRMED once the background commit completes, so the confirmation the user eventually sees is driven entirely by the durable outcome.

sections.s6_takeaway:
When a product manager asks to show "payment confirmed" before the transaction is durably committed, I push back clearly, because the request conflates feeling fast with being correct, and for money correctness has to win. A payment is not real until the transaction that moves the money and records it has durably committed, and before that commit the operation can still fail many ways: insufficient funds discovered late, a constraint violation, a last-minute fraud rejection, a dropped connection, or a crash that rolls the transaction back. If I showed confirmed and then the commit failed, I would have told the user something false, and in payments that false positive is severe and asymmetric because the user may ship goods or stop chasing a bill based on a confirmation that never happened, which is far worse than a slightly slower honest message.

So the design principle I propose is that the user-facing confirmation must always be driven by the real committed outcome. For a fast synchronous payment that means accept the request, perform the charge, wait for the database commit to return success, and only then respond with confirmed, and if the commit rolls back respond with an honest failure the user can act on. The confirmation and the commit are causally linked, so the UI can never display something the system does not durably believe.

For long-running work, where the payment involves slow external gateways, SWIFT, or multi-service orchestration, I do not hold the UI hostage to a confirmation that might take seconds or minutes. Instead I return 202 Accepted immediately with an explicit pending or processing state and a handle like a status URL, and the client either polls that status or receives a push notification or webhook when it completes. The key is that the status transitions from pending to confirmed only when the durable commit of the final step has actually happened, and to failed if it did not, so even asynchronously the confirmation is still driven by the committed outcome; I have only decoupled acknowledging receipt from confirming success. I make the pending state explicit so the user does not take irreversible action prematurely, I keep the status store durable so a crash does not lose it, and I make the transition idempotent and derived from the committed record so a duplicate webhook can never flip a failed payment to confirmed.

On my project at National Bank of India we faced exactly this request, and some optimistically-confirmed payments later failed the final fraud commit, leaving customers believing they had paid and creating reconciliation tickets. We reworked it so fast payments confirm only after the commit returns, failed commits show an honest failure with nothing charged, and international transfers return 202 with a pending state that the app polls and that flips to confirmed only on the durable SWIFT outcome, with a push notification on completion. The app still felt responsive because of the immediate 202, but it never again told a customer a payment succeeded when it had not.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that confirming before the durable commit is dangerous because a rollback makes the confirmation a lie with expensive real-world consequences, so I confirm only on the real committed outcome, and for slow work I return 202 with an explicit pending state the client polls or is notified about, with the final confirmation always derived idempotently from the committed record.

answers.question: How do you implement concurrency control for the "last item / last ticket" problem as a progression — `synchronized`/`ReentrantLock`/`AtomicInteger`/`ConcurrentHashMap` (single JVM only) → DB optimistic/pessimistic locking → Redis distributed lock (`SETNX` + TTL) across many instances → a queue that serializes requests to one consumer (no locks needed)?
answers.shortTitle: How do you implement concurrency control for the "last item / last ticket" problem as a progression

s1_definition.profdef: The "last item" or "last ticket" problem is ensuring that a single remaining unit is sold to exactly one of many concurrent requesters. The solution is a progression of techniques matched to deployment scope: in-process primitives like `synchronized`, `ReentrantLock`, `AtomicInteger`, or `ConcurrentHashMap` work only within one JVM; database optimistic or pessimistic locking works across many instances sharing one database; a Redis distributed lock with `SETNX` plus a TTL works across instances that do not share a lockable row; and serializing all requests through a queue to a single consumer removes the need for locks entirely.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India is giving away one last festival gift voucher and a hundred customers reach for it at once. If it is a single counter, the teller just uses one hand, no coordination needed, which is like in-JVM locking. If there are many counters sharing one ledger, each teller must check and mark the ledger carefully so two tellers cannot both give it away, which is database locking. If the counters do not share a ledger, they agree on a single talking stick that only one teller can hold, which is the Redis lock. Or the bank simply forms one line that funnels every request to one teller who hands out the voucher in order, which is the queue.
s1_definition.oneliner: For the last unit, use in-JVM locks within one process, database optimistic or pessimistic locking across instances sharing a database, a Redis SETNX lock across instances that do not, or a single-consumer queue that serializes requests so no lock is needed at all.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The "last item" or "last ticket" problem is ensuring that a single remaining unit is sold to exactly one of many concurrent requesters. The solution is a progression of techniques matched to deployment scope: in-process primitives like `synchronized`, `ReentrantLock`, `AtomicInteger`, or `ConcurrentHashMap` work only within one JVM; database optimistic or pessimistic locking works across many instances sharing one database; a Redis distributed lock with `SETNX` plus a TTL works across instances that do not share a lockable row; and serializing all requests through a queue to a single consumer removes the need for locks entirely.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India is giving away one last festival gift voucher and a hundred customers reach for it at once. If it is a single counter, the teller just uses one hand, no coordination needed, which is like in-JVM locking. If there are many counters sharing one ledger, each teller must check and mark the ledger carefully so two tellers cannot both give it away, which is database locking. If the counters do not share a ledger, they agree on a single talking stick that only one teller can hold, which is the Redis lock. Or the bank simply forms one line that funnels every request to one teller who hands out the voucher in order, which is the queue.

**One line to remember:** For the last unit, use in-JVM locks within one process, database optimistic or pessimistic locking across instances sharing a database, a Redis SETNX lock across instances that do not, or a single-consumer queue that serializes requests so no lock is needed at all.

sections.s2_technical:
The problem is a check-then-act race: every request reads "stock equals one", all decide they can take it, and all decrement, oversELLING to several buyers. Every technique in the progression exists to make the check-and-decrement atomic at a particular scope, and you climb the progression as your deployment grows.

The first rung is in-process concurrency primitives, which only work when exactly one JVM owns the resource. `synchronized` or a `ReentrantLock` serializes the critical section so only one thread checks and decrements at a time. An `AtomicInteger` lets you do a lock-free compare-and-set, for example `if (stock.compareAndSet(1, 0)) grant(); else reject();`, which atomically takes the last unit only if it is still one. A `ConcurrentHashMap` with atomic methods like `compute` or `putIfAbsent` serializes per key. These are the fastest option and are perfect for a single-instance service, but they are useless the moment you run two instances, because each JVM has its own lock and its own AtomicInteger, so both can sell the last unit.

The second rung is database locking, which works across many application instances because they all share one database, and the database becomes the single point of coordination. Optimistic locking uses a version column: you read the stock and its version, then update with `UPDATE stock SET qty=qty-1, version=version+1 WHERE id=? AND version=?`, and if another transaction already decremented, the version no longer matches, zero rows update, and you retry or reject. It is ideal when conflicts are rare. Pessimistic locking takes a row lock up front with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, so a second transaction blocks until the first commits, then sees the updated stock. It is ideal when contention is high and you prefer waiting over retrying. A simpler and very robust variant is a conditional atomic update, `UPDATE stock SET qty=qty-1 WHERE id=? AND qty>0`, which grants the unit only if stock remains, in one atomic statement.

The third rung is a Redis distributed lock, which you use when instances must coordinate but there is no single lockable database row, for example a one-time external coupon or a resource spread across stores. You acquire a lock with `SET lockKey token NX PX ttl`, where NX means set only if absent so only one caller wins, and PX sets a TTL so a crashed holder's lock expires rather than deadlocking forever. The winner performs the critical operation and releases the lock by deleting it, ideally checking the token so you only delete your own lock. The senior cautions are real: a TTL that is too short can expire mid-operation and let a second holder in, so for strict correctness you use the Redlock algorithm or, better, fence the operation with a monotonic token the resource checks. Because of these hazards you prefer a database constraint over a Redis lock whenever the resource is a row you can constrain.

The fourth rung removes locking entirely by serializing requests through a queue to a single consumer. Every purchase request is published to a queue, and exactly one consumer processes them one at a time in order, decrementing the stock with no contention because there is only ever one actor touching it. This trades some latency and throughput for the simplest possible correctness story and naturally gives you fairness, backpressure, and an audit trail. It is the right choice for extremely high contention flash sales, where even database locks would thrash, because the queue absorbs the spike and the single consumer never races with anyone. The overarching principle is to use the cheapest technique whose scope matches your deployment, and only climb the progression when scaling out breaks the previous rung.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India offers one last discounted fixed-deposit slot and a single-instance service sold it twice under load because two threads both saw one slot. This is exactly the in-JVM rung, where an AtomicInteger compare-and-set takes the last slot only if it is still available.

Problem 2 — When the service scaled to many instances, the in-JVM guard failed because each instance had its own counter. This is exactly the database rung, where a conditional atomic update on the shared stock row enforces single-winner across all instances.

Problem 3 — For a one-time external festival coupon that is not a database row, instances still had to coordinate. This is exactly the Redis-lock rung with SETNX plus TTL.

Problem 4 — During a flash sale the database locks thrashed under extreme contention. This is exactly the queue rung, serializing every request to one consumer.

Our mini-project demonstrates all four rungs. The code defines an `InJvmStock` using AtomicInteger compare-and-set, a `DbStock` using a conditional atomic decrement, a `RedisLock` simulation with SETNX and TTL guarding a coupon, and a `QueueStock` that serializes claims through a single consumer, plus a demo that fires many concurrent buyers at each and shows exactly one winner for the last unit.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one last unit, fifty concurrent buyers released at the same instant, at each rung.

Step 1: At rung one, fifty threads call the in-JVM claim. Each reads the current stock and attempts a compare-and-set from one to zero. Exactly one compare-and-set succeeds because the value can only transition once; the other forty-nine see zero and are rejected. One winner, within this single JVM.

Step 2: At rung two, the same fifty buyers hit the database conditional decrement, simulated by a synchronized row. The first to enter decrements from one to zero and succeeds; every other sees quantity zero and the conditional update affects zero rows, so they are rejected. One winner, and this holds across many instances because they share the one row.

Step 3: At rung three, the coupon has no stock row, so buyers contend on a Redis SETNX lock. One caller sets the key and enters the critical section to redeem, while others fail the NX set and are rejected; the TTL ensures a crashed holder does not deadlock the coupon. One winner across instances.

Step 4: At rung four, all fifty requests are placed on a queue and a single consumer processes them one by one. The consumer grants the first request because stock is one, then rejects the rest because stock is zero, with no lock anywhere because only one actor ever touches the stock. One winner.

Step 5: Every rung reports exactly one winner for the last unit, demonstrating that each technique enforces single-winner at its own scope and that the right rung depends on the deployment.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The last-item or last-ticket problem is fundamentally a check-then-act race: many concurrent requests all read that one unit remains, all decide they can take it, and all decrement, so you oversell. Every technique I use exists to make that check-and-decrement atomic at a particular scope, and I describe the solution as a progression where I climb one rung at a time as the deployment grows, always using the cheapest technique whose scope matches the system.

The first rung is in-process primitives, which only work inside a single JVM. A synchronized block or a ReentrantLock serializes the critical section, and an AtomicInteger lets me do a lock-free compare-and-set that takes the last unit only if it is still one, with a ConcurrentHashMap serializing per key. These are the fastest option and perfect for a single instance, but they are useless the instant I run two instances, because each JVM has its own lock and its own counter, so both can sell the last unit. That failure is exactly what pushes me to the second rung.

The second rung is database locking, which works across many instances because they share one database that becomes the single coordinator. Optimistic locking uses a version column and an update guarded by that version, so a losing transaction updates zero rows and retries, which suits rare conflicts. Pessimistic locking takes a row lock with SELECT FOR UPDATE so a second transaction blocks until the first commits, which suits high contention. In practice the most robust form is a single conditional atomic update that decrements only where quantity is greater than zero. When instances must coordinate but there is no lockable row, for example a one-time external coupon, I climb to the third rung, a Redis distributed lock using SET with NX and a PX TTL, where NX makes only the first caller win and the TTL prevents a crashed holder from deadlocking the resource forever, and for strict correctness I add a fencing token. The fourth rung removes locking entirely: I push every request onto a queue and let a single consumer process them one at a time, so there is only ever one actor touching the stock and no contention exists, which is the right choice for extreme flash-sale contention because the queue absorbs the spike and also gives fairness, backpressure, and an audit trail.

On my project at National Bank of India I actually walked this progression. A single-instance service sold one last discounted fixed-deposit slot twice, so I started with an AtomicInteger compare-and-set. When we scaled out, that broke because each instance had its own counter, so I moved to a conditional atomic decrement on the shared stock row. For a one-time festival coupon that was not a database row, I used a Redis SETNX lock with a TTL. And during a flash sale when even database locks thrashed, I serialized claims through a Kafka topic to a single consumer. The guiding rule I always state is to prefer a database constraint over a distributed lock whenever the resource is a row I can constrain, because the lock's TTL and expiry hazards are real.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I enforce single-winner for the last unit with in-JVM compare-and-set within one process, database optimistic or pessimistic locking across instances sharing a database, a Redis SETNX-plus-TTL lock across instances with no lockable row, or a single-consumer queue that serializes requests so no lock is needed, and I pick the rung by matching its scope to the deployment and climb only when scaling out breaks the previous one.

answers.question: How do you make a message/event consumer safe against at-least-once duplicate delivery (store a `processed_event_id` / inbox table and skip already-processed IDs, use unique DB constraints, or idempotent state transitions) — and why is "do not corrupt state on reprocessing" the real goal rather than literal exactly-once?
answers.shortTitle: How do you make a message/event consumer safe against at-least-once duplicate delivery

s1_definition.profdef: You make a consumer safe against at-least-once duplicate delivery by making processing idempotent: store each processed event id in an inbox table and skip events already present, enforce a unique database constraint on a natural key so a duplicate insert fails atomically, or use idempotent state transitions that are no-ops when the resource is already in the target state. The real goal is not literal exactly-once delivery, which is practically impossible across independent systems, but ensuring that reprocessing the same event never corrupts state, which gives you effectively-once semantics.
s1_definition.analogy: When the back office at National Bank of India gets a "credit Priya 50000" instruction, it first checks a logbook of instruction numbers it has already handled. If this number is in the logbook, it ignores the instruction and moves on, so even if the mail room delivers the same letter twice, Priya is credited only once. The bank does not try to make the postal service magically deliver each letter exactly once; it just makes sure that handling a letter twice has the same effect as handling it once.
s1_definition.oneliner: Make the consumer idempotent with an inbox of processed event ids, a unique constraint, or no-op state transitions, because the achievable and correct goal is that reprocessing never corrupts state, not literal exactly-once delivery.

The real goal is not literal exactly-once delivery, which is practically impossible across independent systems, but ensuring that reprocessing the same event never corrupts state, which gives you effectively-once semantics.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When the back office at National Bank of India gets a "credit Priya 50000" instruction, it first checks a logbook of instruction numbers it has already handled. If this number is in the logbook, it ignores the instruction and moves on, so even if the mail room delivers the same letter twice, Priya is credited only once. sections.s2_technical:
Start with why exactly-once delivery is the wrong target. Across independent systems, a broker and a consumer, there is always a moment where the consumer has processed a message but its acknowledgment to the broker is lost, so the broker, unable to know the message was handled, redelivers it. You cannot eliminate this without a perfect distributed agreement that the physics of unreliable networks forbids. So brokers offer at-least-once delivery, which guarantees no message is lost but allows duplicates. Chasing literal exactly-once is chasing a mirage; what you can achieve, and what actually matters, is that processing a duplicate has no additional effect, which people call effectively-once or exactly-once processing.

The first technique is the inbox or processed-event table. You keep a table of processed event ids, and before applying an event you check whether its id is already there; if it is, you skip. The crucial detail is that the check and the insert of the id must be atomic and must commit in the same transaction as the business change. If you check, then process, then record the id as separate steps, a crash in between lets a redelivery reprocess. So you do `INSERT INTO inbox(event_id) VALUES(?)` guarded by a unique constraint and, in the same transaction, perform the business update; if the insert fails as a duplicate, you roll back and skip, because someone already processed this event. This single-transaction coupling is what makes it correct under both duplicates and crashes.

The second technique is a unique database constraint on a natural business key, which is often simpler than a separate inbox. If each event produces a record with a naturally unique key, for example a settlement with a unique trade id, you put a unique constraint on that key and let the duplicate insert fail. The database atomically rejects the second one, and you treat the duplicate-key error as "already processed". This is extremely robust because the guarantee lives in the database and needs no extra lookup.

The third technique is idempotent state transitions, which suit events that drive a state machine. If an event means "move this order to SHIPPED", then applying it when the order is already SHIPPED is a no-op, so reprocessing is harmless by construction. You implement this with a conditional update, for example `UPDATE orders SET status='SHIPPED' WHERE id=? AND status='PLACED'`, which affects one row the first time and zero rows on a duplicate, so the duplicate changes nothing. This needs no inbox at all when the domain already has clear states.

Several senior points round this out. Choose the technique by shape: inbox for general side effects, unique constraint for inserts, state transition for state machines, and often a combination. The id you dedupe on must identify the logical event, not the delivery attempt, and it must be stable across redeliveries. Non-database side effects, like sending an email or calling an external API, are harder because you cannot wrap them in the database transaction, so you either make them idempotent downstream, use the inbox to guard them, or accept at-most-once for truly non-idempotent external calls. You should also prune the inbox with a retention window so it does not grow forever, sized to the maximum redelivery horizon. And the same reasoning is why the real engineering statement is "do not corrupt state on reprocessing": it frames the problem around the invariant you can actually guarantee rather than a delivery property you cannot.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A consumer at National Bank of India credited Priya from a `MoneyCredited` event, then the broker redelivered the same event after a lost acknowledgment, and Priya was credited twice. This is exactly why we need an inbox of processed event ids checked and written in the same transaction as the credit.

Problem 2 — A settlement consumer inserted a settlement row per event and a duplicate event created two rows. This is exactly why a unique constraint on the trade id rejects the duplicate atomically.

Problem 3 — An order-status consumer received a duplicate "ship" event. This is exactly why an idempotent conditional transition makes the second delivery a no-op.

Our mini-project builds a safe consumer demonstrating all three. The code defines an `InboxStore` for processed ids, a `BalanceStore` credited idempotently via the inbox, a `SettlementStore` with a unique trade-id guard, an `OrderStore` with a conditional state transition, and a demo that delivers each event twice to prove reprocessing never corrupts state.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: event EVT-1 crediting CUR3001 by 50000 delivered twice; settlement TRD-7 delivered twice; order ORD-9 shipped twice.

Step 1: EVT-1 arrives. The consumer claims the event id in the inbox atomically and, in the same transaction, credits Priya from 250000 to 300000. The inbox now contains EVT-1.

Step 2: EVT-1 is redelivered. The inbox claim fails because EVT-1 is already present, so the consumer skips the credit entirely. Priya's balance stays at 300000, so the duplicate did not corrupt state.

Step 3: Settlement TRD-7 arrives and inserts a row because the trade id is new. The redelivered TRD-7 fails the unique trade-id constraint, so it is rejected and no second row is created; the row count stays at one.

Step 4: Order ORD-9 is placed, then a ship event transitions it from PLACED to SHIPPED. The duplicate ship event finds the status already SHIPPED, so the conditional transition is a no-op and the status is unchanged.

Step 5: Across all three techniques, the second delivery of each event produced no additional effect, which is the real goal: reprocessing never corrupted state, delivering effectively-once semantics without ever requiring literal exactly-once delivery.

sections.s6_takeaway:
I always begin by reframing the problem, because the framing is the answer. Literal exactly-once delivery is the wrong target: across a broker and a consumer there is always a moment where the consumer has processed a message but its acknowledgment is lost, so the broker cannot know and redelivers, and no amount of engineering removes that without a perfect distributed agreement the physics of unreliable networks forbids. So brokers give at-least-once delivery, which never loses a message but allows duplicates, and the achievable, correct goal is that reprocessing a duplicate has no additional effect. That is why the real engineering statement is do not corrupt state on reprocessing, and people call the result effectively-once.

To achieve that I make the consumer idempotent with one of three techniques chosen by the shape of the work. The inbox technique keeps a table of processed event ids, and before applying an event I atomically claim its id and, in the same transaction as the business change, commit both; if the id is already present I skip. The critical detail is the single transaction, because if I checked, processed, and recorded the id as separate steps, a crash in between would let a redelivery reprocess. The unique-constraint technique puts a unique index on a natural business key, like a trade id, and lets the duplicate insert fail atomically, which is wonderfully robust because the database enforces it with no extra lookup. The state-transition technique suits events that drive a state machine, where I use a conditional update that moves an order from placed to shipped only if it is still placed, so a duplicate affects zero rows and changes nothing.

The senior points I add are that I pick the technique by shape, often combining them, that the id I dedupe on must identify the logical event and be stable across redeliveries rather than identifying the delivery attempt, and that non-database side effects like emails or external API calls are harder because I cannot put them in the database transaction, so I make them idempotent downstream, guard them with the inbox, or accept at-most-once for truly non-idempotent external calls. I also prune the inbox with a retention window sized to the maximum redelivery horizon so it does not grow forever.

On my project at National Bank of India this came straight from incidents. A consumer credited Priya, lost its acknowledgment, and on redelivery credited her twice, so we added an inbox check and the credit committed in the same transaction. A settlement consumer created duplicate rows on a redelivered event, so we added a unique constraint on the trade id. And an order consumer received a duplicate ship event, which we made harmless with a conditional transition. In every case the fix was not to chase exactly-once delivery but to guarantee that handling an event twice left the system in exactly the same state as handling it once.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I make a consumer safe against at-least-once duplicates with an inbox of processed event ids committed in the same transaction as the business change, a unique constraint on a natural key, or an idempotent state transition, because the goal I can actually guarantee, and the one that matters, is that reprocessing never corrupts state, not literal exactly-once delivery.

s1_definition.profdef: The naive check-then-act dedup fails in two distinct ways. Under concurrency, two consumers both call `alreadyProcessed(id)`, both see false, and both process, because the gap between the check and the mark is a race window. On crash, a consumer processes the business change but crashes before `markProcessed(id)`, so on redelivery the id is still unmarked and the work is re-applied. The two fixes are to make the dedup write atomic with a unique constraint on the event id so only one consumer can win the insert, and to commit the business update and the dedup record in the same database transaction so a crash cannot separate them.
s1_definition.analogy: Two clerks at National Bank of India both glance at the logbook, both see the instruction number is not logged yet, and both credit Priya, because the glance and the pen-stroke were separate actions with a gap between them. Separately, one clerk credits Priya but faints before writing the number in the logbook, so when the instruction comes again it looks brand new and Priya is credited twice. The fix is a logbook that physically allows each number to be written only once so only one clerk wins, and doing the credit and the logbook entry as one inseparable action so fainting cannot split them.

sections.s2_technical:
Look closely at the naive code: `if (!alreadyProcessed(id)) { process(); markProcessed(id); }`. It has three separate operations, a read, a side effect, and a write, with no atomicity binding them, and both failure modes live in the gaps between them.

The concurrency failure is a classic check-then-act race. Two consumers in a consumer group, or the same message delivered to two instances, both execute `alreadyProcessed(id)` at nearly the same time. Because neither has marked the id yet, both reads return false. Both then proceed into `process()`, applying the business effect twice, and both call `markProcessed(id)` afterward. The read and the subsequent write are not a single atomic operation, so there is a window in which both consumers believe they are the first. No amount of ordering the three lines differently fixes this; the problem is that the decision and the claim are not atomic.

The crash failure is about the gap between `process()` and `markProcessed(id)`. Suppose a single consumer runs `process()`, which applies the business change, and then the process is killed before `markProcessed(id)` executes. The business effect is already applied, but the id was never marked. When the broker redelivers the message, because at-least-once delivery guarantees it will, the consumer runs `alreadyProcessed(id)`, sees false because the mark never happened, and re-applies the business change. Even if the two writes are in the right order, a crash between them re-applies the work.

The first fix makes the dedup write atomic so the claim itself decides the winner. Instead of reading then writing, you attempt a single atomic insert of the event id into a table with a unique constraint, `INSERT INTO inbox(event_id) VALUES(?)` where `event_id` is `UNIQUE`. The database guarantees only one insert of a given id can succeed; the concurrent second consumer's insert fails with a duplicate-key error. So you process only if your insert succeeded, and you treat the duplicate-key error as "someone else owns this event, skip". This collapses the check-then-act window into one atomic operation that the database arbitrates, which is the only reliable arbiter under concurrency.

The second fix binds the business update and the dedup record into one database transaction so a crash cannot separate them. You do `BEGIN; INSERT INTO inbox(event_id) ...; <business update>; COMMIT;`. Now there are only two possible outcomes: either the transaction commits, in which case both the mark and the business change are durably present together, or it does not commit, in which case neither is, and a redelivery can safely redo the whole thing. There is no state where the business change is applied but the id is unmarked, which is exactly the state that caused the crash double-processing. The two fixes are complementary: the unique constraint handles concurrency by picking one winner, and the single transaction handles crashes by making the mark and the effect atomic.

Senior nuances: the business update must be in the same transactional resource as the inbox for the single-transaction guarantee to hold, which is straightforward when both are in the same database but requires the transactional outbox or careful design when the side effect is external, like sending an email, since you cannot enlist an email in a database transaction. In that case you record intent in the transaction and perform the external effect idempotently afterward. Also, you acknowledge the message to the broker only after the transaction commits, so a crash before commit simply causes a safe redelivery. This pattern is the transactional inbox, the consumer-side mirror of the transactional outbox.
