answers.question: How would you migrate master data from a legacy system to a custom cloud-based solution (API design, cloud storage, ETL migration, DB setup, monitoring, security, CI/CD)?
answers.shortTitle: How would you migrate master data from a legacy system to a custom cloud-based solution

s1_definition.profdef: A master data migration moves the authoritative reference records of a business, such as customers, accounts, products, and branch details, from an older on-premise system to a newly built cloud platform. It is an ETL pipeline, extract from the legacy source, transform into the new schema while cleaning and validating, and load into the cloud database, executed in controlled phases with reconciliation. Done well it uses staging in cloud object storage, idempotent batch loads, parallel-run validation, strong security over data in transit and at rest, observability on every record, and an automated CI/CD pipeline so the migration tooling itself is tested and repeatable.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India is moving from an old paper-and-mainframe records room to a brand new digital vault in the cloud. The old room holds the master ledgers: every customer like Rajesh and Priya, their account numbers, balances, and KYC details. You cannot just dump the papers into the new vault. You photograph each record (extract), correct smudges and reformat it to the new vault's filing standard (transform), then file it neatly in the new vault (load). You keep the old room open and compare both for a while (parallel run) until you are certain the new vault is perfect, and only then close the old room.
s1_definition.oneliner: Extract, transform, load, reconcile, and parallel-run, treating the migration as idempotent, secure, observable, and automated rather than a one-shot copy.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A master data migration moves the authoritative reference records of a business, such as customers, accounts, products, and branch details, from an older on-premise system to a newly built cloud platform. It is an ETL pipeline, extract from the legacy source, transform into the new schema while cleaning and validating, and load into the cloud database, executed in controlled phases with reconciliation. Done well it uses staging in cloud object storage, idempotent batch loads, parallel-run validation, strong security over data in transit and at rest, observability on every record, and an automated CI/CD pipeline so the migration tooling itself is tested and repeatable.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India is moving from an old paper-and-mainframe records room to a brand new digital vault in the cloud. The old room holds the master ledgers: every customer like Rajesh and Priya, their account numbers, balances, and KYC details. You cannot just dump the papers into the new vault. You photograph each record (extract), correct smudges and reformat it to the new vault's filing standard (transform), then file it neatly in the new vault (load). You keep the old room open and compare both for a while (parallel run) until you are certain the new vault is perfect, and only then close the old room.

**One line to remember:** Extract, transform, load, reconcile, and parallel-run, treating the migration as idempotent, secure, observable, and automated rather than a one-shot copy.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with discovery and data profiling. Before moving anything, you profile the legacy data: how many customers, how many accounts, what formats, where the nulls and duplicates and encoding problems are. Legacy systems accumulate decades of dirty data: dates stored as strings, phone numbers in five formats, duplicate customer records. You cannot design the transform until you know the mess you are moving.

Next, schema design in the cloud. You design the target database for the new model, not a mirror of the old one. For master data you often choose a relational database such as Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL or Cloud SQL because master data has strong integrity rules, foreign keys, and needs transactions. You define the tables, constraints, and indexes, and you write the DDL as versioned migrations with a tool like Flyway or Liquibase so the schema is reproducible.

The migration itself is an ETL pipeline. Extract reads from the legacy source, often a nightly database dump, a replica, or change data capture if you need near-real-time. Rather than reading the legacy production database directly under load, you export to cloud object storage first, such as Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage, as the landing and staging zone. Staging in object storage gives you a durable, cheap, replayable copy, so if the load fails you re-run from staging without touching legacy again. Transform cleans, deduplicates, standardizes formats, maps old codes to new codes, and validates each record against business rules such as "balance must be non-negative" and "account must reference a valid customer." Load writes the transformed records into the cloud database in batches.

Idempotency is essential. The load must be safe to run twice, because migrations get interrupted. You achieve this with upserts keyed on a stable natural or legacy key, so re-running updates existing rows rather than creating duplicates. You also checkpoint progress so a restart resumes from the last committed batch rather than from zero.

API design matters because the new cloud platform exposes master data through services. You design clean REST or gRPC APIs such as `GET /api/v1/customers/{id}` and `GET /api/v1/accounts/{id}`, versioned from day one, so consumers migrate off the legacy interfaces onto the new ones. During transition you may run an anti-corruption layer or facade that lets old consumers keep calling familiar endpoints while the data lives in the new store.

Reconciliation and parallel run prove correctness. After loading, you compare counts and checksums: number of customers, sum of balances, record-level hashes between legacy and cloud. You run both systems in parallel, serving reads from the new system while continuing to validate against the old, and you only cut over writes when reconciliation is clean. You always keep a rollback plan.

Security is non-negotiable for banking master data. Data in transit uses TLS. Data at rest is encrypted with KMS-managed keys. Access to staging buckets and the database is least-privilege IAM. Personally identifiable information and KYC fields may be tokenized or masked in non-production environments. Every access is audited.

Monitoring and observability track the migration per record: how many extracted, transformed, loaded, rejected, and why. You emit metrics to Prometheus or CloudWatch, dashboards in Grafana, and alerts when the rejection rate crosses a threshold. A rejected-records table captures every row that failed validation with its reason so operators can fix and replay.

Finally, CI/CD. The migration code, schema migrations, and infrastructure are in version control. A pipeline runs unit tests on the transform logic, runs the schema migrations against a test database, executes a dry run against a sample, and deploys the tooling. The migration is not a hand-run script on someone's laptop; it is a tested, repeatable, automated artifact.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India is retiring a thirty-year-old mainframe that holds master data for customers and accounts, including Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001), and moving to a cloud platform on AWS.

Problem 1 — the legacy data is dirty. Balances are stored as strings with commas like "1,000,000.00", account statuses use cryptic single letters, and some customer rows are duplicated. If we load this as-is, the new system has wrong balances and duplicate customers. This is why we need a transform step that cleans, parses to BigDecimal, maps codes, and deduplicates before loading.

Problem 2 — the migration got interrupted halfway last time and created duplicates on restart. We re-ran it and loaded Rajesh twice. This is why the load must be idempotent: it upserts on the legacy key, so re-running updates rather than duplicates, and checkpoints so it resumes.

Problem 3 — nobody trusted the new numbers. After the first attempt, finance asked "does the total deposits in the cloud equal the mainframe total?" and we could not answer. This is why we need reconciliation: compare record counts and the sum of all balances between source and target before cutover.

The mini-project builds a runnable ETL demo: a `LegacyRecord` representing raw mainframe rows, an `Extractor` that reads them, a `Transformer` that cleans and validates into a `CustomerAccount`, an idempotent `Loader` simulating upsert into the cloud database, a `RejectedStore` for bad rows, and a `Reconciler` that compares source and target. It migrates Rajesh and Priya plus one dirty duplicate and one invalid row.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four legacy rows. Rajesh (valid), Priya (valid), Rajesh again (duplicate), and a bad row with a negative balance and unknown KYC.

Step 1: Extract reads all four rows from staging. In production these come from an S3 export of the mainframe dump, not the live mainframe.

Step 2: Row 1, Rajesh. Transform splits the pipe-delimited line, maps KYC code V to VERIFIED, type S to SAVINGS, status A to ACTIVE, and parses "1,000,000.00" by stripping the comma into a BigDecimal. All validations pass. Load upserts SAV2001 as an INSERT.

Step 3: Row 2, Priya. Same clean path. Type C maps to CURRENT. Load inserts CUR3001.

Step 4: Row 3, Rajesh duplicate. Transform succeeds identically. Load calls upsert on SAV2001, which already exists, so it becomes an UPDATE, not a second row. This is idempotency in action: the duplicate did not create a duplicate record.

Step 5: Row 4, bad row. Transform parses the balance as negative and throws ValidationException "negative balance not allowed". The loader never sees it. It goes to the RejectedStore with its reason, and a severe log is written.

Step 6: Reconcile computes the source total of unique valid balances (1,000,000 + 250,000 = 1,250,000) and compares it to the loaded total (also 1,250,000). They match, so it logs RECONCILE OK.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] INSERTED SAV2001 (Rajesh Kumar, balance=1000000.00)
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] INSERTED CUR3001 (Priya Sharma, balance=250000.00)
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] UPDATED SAV2001 (Rajesh Kumar, balance=1000000.00)
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [SEVERE ] REJECTED [negative balance not allowed] : CUST03|Bad Row|Unknown|X|ACC9999|S|-500.00|A
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] RECONCILE OK — source total = target total = 1250000.00
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] Loaded accounts = 2, rejected = 1
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To migrate master data from a legacy system to a custom cloud platform, I treat it as a controlled ETL pipeline with reconciliation and a parallel run, not a one-shot copy. I begin with discovery and data profiling, because legacy systems accumulate decades of dirty data such as balances stored as comma-separated strings, cryptic status codes, and duplicate customer rows, and I cannot design a correct transform until I understand that mess. Then I design the target schema for the new model with proper constraints and versioned migrations using Flyway, so the cloud database is reproducible rather than a blind mirror of the old one.

The pipeline itself extracts from the legacy source into cloud object storage such as S3 as a durable, replayable staging zone, so if a load fails I re-run from staging without ever touching the fragile legacy system again. The transform step cleans, parses amounts into BigDecimal, maps old codes to new codes, deduplicates, and validates each record against business rules like non-negative balances and valid KYC. The load step writes to the cloud database in batches, and critically it is idempotent: it upserts on a stable key and checkpoints progress, so if the migration is interrupted and restarted it updates existing rows instead of creating duplicates. On an earlier attempt we did not have this and a restart loaded Rajesh twice, which is exactly the failure idempotency prevents.

I prove correctness with reconciliation and a parallel run. After loading I compare record counts and the sum of all balances between source and target, and I only trust the migration when the numbers match exactly, which is the answer finance always demands. I keep the old system live, serve reads from the new one while continuously validating against the old, and cut over writes only when reconciliation is clean, always with a rollback plan. I expose the migrated data through clean versioned REST APIs, and during transition I front it with an anti-corruption facade so existing consumers keep working while they migrate.

Security and automation wrap everything. For banking master data I encrypt in transit with TLS and at rest with KMS keys, lock down staging buckets and the database with least-privilege IAM, mask PII in non-production, and audit every access. Observability tracks each record as extracted, transformed, loaded, or rejected, with a rejects table capturing every bad row and its reason so operators can fix and replay, and alerts fire when the rejection rate spikes. The whole migration lives in CI/CD: the transform logic is unit tested, the schema migrations run against a test database, a dry run executes on a sample, and the tooling and infrastructure deploy as versioned, tested artifacts rather than a hand-run script on someone's laptop.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that master data migration is an idempotent, reconciled ETL pipeline that stages in cloud object storage, cleans and validates on the way in, upserts safely so restarts never duplicate, proves itself by matching counts and balance totals between source and target, runs the old and new systems in parallel before cutover, and is fully secured, observed, and automated through CI/CD.

answers.question: Design a microservice to handle uploading large files (100MB+) under high concurrency (streaming, presigned URLs, async metadata queue, reactive WebFlux, backpressure/rate limiting).
answers.shortTitle: Design a microservice to handle uploading large files (100MB+) under high concurrency

s1_definition.profdef: A large-file upload microservice accepts files of a hundred megabytes or more from many clients at once without exhausting server memory or threads. The key design moves are: never buffer the whole file in memory, instead stream it; prefer offloading the actual bytes to object storage directly from the client using presigned URLs so the application server handles only control-plane requests; process file metadata asynchronously through a message queue; use a reactive, non-blocking stack such as Spring WebFlux so a few threads serve thousands of concurrent uploads; and apply backpressure and rate limiting so a flood of uploads cannot overwhelm downstream systems.
s1_definition.analogy: Customers of National Bank of India need to upload large documents: scanned loan files, years of statements, KYC videos. Imagine the branch clerk trying to personally carry every customer's heavy suitcase into the vault. With one clerk and a thousand customers, the clerk collapses. Instead, the bank gives each customer a one-time pass (presigned URL) to drive their own suitcase straight to the warehouse (object storage) through a loading dock, while the clerk only writes down "Rajesh dropped off suitcase 7 at 3pm" on a slip and puts that slip in an in-tray (queue) for later filing. The clerk never lifts a suitcase, so one clerk serves thousands.
s1_definition.oneliner: Don't move big bytes through your server; mint a presigned URL so the client uploads straight to object storage, and handle only lightweight metadata asynchronously on a non-blocking stack.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A large-file upload microservice accepts files of a hundred megabytes or more from many clients at once without exhausting server memory or threads. **In simple words (banking analogy):** Customers of National Bank of India need to upload large documents: scanned loan files, years of statements, KYC videos. sections.s2_technical:
The first principle is never buffer a large file in memory. A naive Spring MVC controller that takes a `MultipartFile` and calls `getBytes()` loads the entire file into the heap. A hundred concurrent 100 MB uploads is 10 GB of heap, which is an instant OutOfMemoryError. Even streaming the `InputStream` through your server still consumes a thread and network bandwidth for the whole duration of each upload, so under high concurrency the thread pool saturates.

The better architecture is to keep the bytes off your server entirely using presigned URLs. Object storage such as Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage can issue a short-lived, cryptographically signed URL that grants permission to upload one specific object for a few minutes. The flow is: the client calls your API `POST /api/v1/uploads` with just the filename and size; your service validates and returns a presigned URL; the client uploads the raw bytes directly to S3 using that URL; S3 stores the object; your service never touches the file content. Your API only handles tiny JSON control requests, so one small instance serves enormous upload volume.

For files in the multi-gigabyte range, a single presigned PUT is not enough, so you use S3 multipart upload: the client splits the file into parts (say 10 MB each), requests a presigned URL per part, uploads parts in parallel, and finally calls a complete step that stitches them together. This also gives resumability: a failed part is retried without re-uploading the whole file.

Metadata is processed asynchronously. When the upload finishes, you record metadata: who uploaded, filename, size, checksum, storage key. You do not do heavy work (virus scan, thumbnail, indexing) inline on the upload request. Instead you drop an event onto a message queue such as Kafka or SQS, and background workers consume it. This decouples the fast upload path from slow processing, so a burst of uploads does not block on scanning.

When you must stream through your own service (for example because the client cannot talk to S3 directly, or you need to inspect bytes in flight), use a reactive, non-blocking stack. Spring WebFlux with `Flux<DataBuffer>` streams the body in chunks without loading it all into memory, and because it is non-blocking, a handful of event-loop threads can serve thousands of simultaneous slow uploads instead of tying up one blocking thread per upload. The `ReactiveHttpInputMessage` body is a `Flux` of buffers that you pipe straight to a reactive S3 client.

Backpressure is the reactive mechanism that stops a fast producer from overwhelming a slow consumer. If the client uploads faster than S3 can accept, the reactive pipeline signals "slow down" upstream rather than buffering unbounded data in memory. WebFlux and reactive S3 clients honour this automatically through the Reactive Streams `request(n)` protocol, so memory stays bounded even under pressure.

Rate limiting protects the system from abuse and overload. You cap how many uploads a single user or the whole system can start per minute, using a token bucket, so a misbehaving client or a traffic spike cannot exhaust storage bandwidth or cost. You also enforce a maximum file size before issuing a presigned URL, so nobody can request a URL for a 50 GB file.

Validation and security matter. You validate the declared content type and, after upload, the actual MIME type from magic bytes rather than trusting the extension, enforce size limits, and scan untrusted content for viruses in the async pipeline before the file is marked usable. Presigned URLs are short-lived and scoped to one object and one operation, so a leaked URL expires quickly.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India lets customers upload large documents for loan applications: Rajesh (SAV2001) uploads a 150 MB scanned property file for a home loan, and thousands of other customers upload simultaneously during a festive loan campaign.

Problem 1 — the server ran out of memory. The first version took a MultipartFile and read all bytes into the heap. During the campaign, a few hundred concurrent 150 MB uploads blew the heap and crashed the service. This is why we must never buffer the whole file: we hand the client a presigned URL and let it upload directly to object storage.

Problem 2 — the upload thread pool saturated. Even after switching to streaming, every slow upload held a blocking thread for minutes, so a few hundred slow mobile uploads exhausted the thread pool and new customers got rejected. This is why we use a reactive non-blocking stack: a few event-loop threads serve thousands of slow uploads.

Problem 3 — virus scanning blocked every upload. The first design scanned the file inline before responding, so each upload waited thirty seconds for the scanner. This is why we process metadata and scanning asynchronously through a queue: the upload finishes fast, and a background worker scans and marks the file usable afterward.

The mini-project builds a runnable demo of the control plane: an `UploadService` that validates a request and issues a presigned URL (simulated), an idempotent metadata record, an async `MetadataQueue` that workers consume for scanning, and a `RateLimiter` using a token bucket. It processes Rajesh's 150 MB request and shows a rejected oversized request and a rate-limited request.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh requests to upload a 150 MB PDF; Priya requests a 500 MB video; Rajesh fires 12 quick 1 MB requests.

Step 1: Rajesh's 150 MB request hits `requestUpload`. The rate limiter grants a token. The size 150 MB is under the 200 MB cap, so it passes.

Step 2: The service asks PresignService for a presigned PUT URL. It gets back a storage key like SAV2001/uuid/property_deed.pdf and a URL valid for five minutes. No file bytes have moved yet.

Step 3: The service records FileMetadata with status UPLOADING and publishes it to the metadata queue, then returns the ticket. The whole API call is tiny and fast.

Step 4: The client (not the server) uploads the 150 MB bytes directly to S3 using the presigned URL. Our service never touches those bytes, so memory and threads are untouched.

Step 5: The background ScanWorker polls the queue, picks up Rajesh's metadata, simulates a virus scan and magic-byte MIME verification, and sets status to SCANNED_CLEAN. This happens off the upload path, so the upload was never blocked by scanning.

Step 6: Priya's 500 MB request hits the size check and throws FileTooLargeException before any URL is issued. No storage, no bandwidth wasted.

Step 7: Rajesh's 12 rapid requests consume his 10 tokens; requests 11 and 12 throw RateLimitedException, protecting the system from a single user flooding it.

sections.s6_takeaway:
To design a microservice for large file uploads under high concurrency, my guiding principle is that big bytes should never flow through my application server. A naive controller that reads a MultipartFile into memory will throw OutOfMemoryError the moment a few hundred clients upload hundred-megabyte files at once, and even streaming through my service still ties up a thread and bandwidth per upload, so the thread pool saturates. The architecture I reach for is presigned URLs: the client calls my API with just the filename, size, and type; I validate it and return a short-lived, signed URL scoped to one object; the client then uploads the raw bytes directly to object storage such as S3; and my service never touches the content. That way one small instance handles enormous upload volume, because it only serves tiny control-plane JSON requests.

For multi-gigabyte files I use S3 multipart upload, where the client splits the file into parts, gets a presigned URL per part, uploads them in parallel, and calls a complete step to stitch them together, which also gives resumability so a failed part is retried without re-uploading the whole file. I process all the heavy work asynchronously: when the upload finishes I record metadata and drop an event on a queue like Kafka, and a background worker fleet does virus scanning, MIME magic-byte verification, and thumbnailing. This decouples the fast upload path from slow processing, which is exactly the fix for the problem where inline scanning made every upload wait thirty seconds.

When I genuinely must stream bytes through my own service, for example to inspect them in flight, I use a reactive non-blocking stack like Spring WebFlux, where the body arrives as a Flux of data buffers that I pipe straight to a reactive storage client without ever holding the whole file in memory. Because the stack is non-blocking, a handful of event-loop threads serve thousands of simultaneous slow uploads instead of one blocking thread each, which solves the thread-pool saturation we hit on mobile. Reactive Streams backpressure keeps memory bounded: if the client uploads faster than storage can accept, the pipeline signals upstream to slow down rather than buffering unbounded data.

On my project at National Bank of India, customers like Rajesh upload 150-megabyte scanned property files during loan campaigns, thousands at once. We moved to presigned direct-to-S3 uploads so the server stopped running out of memory, processed metadata and scanning through a queue so uploads finished fast, and put the control plane on WebFlux so a few threads handled the concurrency. We enforce a maximum file size before issuing any URL so nobody can request a URL for a 50-gigabyte file, and a per-user token-bucket rate limit so one client cannot flood storage bandwidth or cost. We validate the real MIME type from magic bytes after upload rather than trusting the extension, and we scan untrusted content before marking a file usable, moving infected files to quarantine.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I keep the bytes off my server by minting short-lived presigned URLs so clients upload straight to object storage, I use multipart upload for very large files, I handle only lightweight metadata on a non-blocking WebFlux stack with backpressure, I push scanning and processing onto an async queue of background workers, and I guard the whole thing with size limits and per-user rate limiting so high concurrency never exhausts memory, threads, or cost.

---

s1_definition.profdef: Routing file bytes through the application server couples your request threads, heap, and local disk to upload size and duration, which does not scale and risks OutOfMemoryError and disk exhaustion. A presigned URL is a time-limited, cryptographically signed URL generated by object storage (S3/GCS) that grants a client permission to perform one specific operation on one specific object, so the client transfers bytes directly to storage while your API only mints the URL. Multi-gigabyte uploads use multipart upload, splitting the object into independently uploaded parts that storage reassembles. You must verify the actual content type from the file's magic bytes rather than its extension, enforce a size limit, and virus-scan untrusted user content, because the extension and declared type are attacker-controlled and meaningless.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, imagine every customer's heavy document box had to pass through the manager's own office. The manager's desk (heap) overflows, the office floor (disk) fills up, and the manager (thread) is stuck holding each box for the whole transfer. Instead the manager writes a one-time gate pass (presigned URL) that lets the customer drive straight to the warehouse (storage). For a truly enormous shipment, the customer splits it into labelled pallets (multipart) that the warehouse stacks back together. And the guard never trusts the label on the box; he opens it and checks what is actually inside (magic bytes) and scans it for anything dangerous (virus scan) before it is accepted.
s1_definition.oneliner: The app server mints a short-lived signed URL and steps aside; bytes go client-to-storage directly, in parts if huge, and you trust the file's actual contents, never its label.

sections.s2_technical:
Why not stream through the app server. Three resources get consumed per upload when bytes pass through your service: heap memory if you buffer, a request thread for the entire upload duration, and local disk if you spool to temp files. A single slow 2 GB upload on a mobile connection can hold a thread for ten minutes. A few hundred concurrent large uploads exhaust the thread pool, blow the heap, or fill the disk, and your service falls over even though it is doing no useful computation, just copying bytes. Your application server should spend its CPU and threads on business logic, not on being a dumb byte pipe that object storage does far better and cheaper.

How a presigned URL works. Object storage like S3 lets an authorized backend generate a URL that embeds a signature computed from your secret credentials, the target bucket and key, the allowed HTTP method, and an expiry time. Anyone holding that URL can perform exactly that one operation until it expires, without any credentials of their own. The flow: the client asks your API to upload a file; your API authenticates the user, validates the request, and calls the S3 presigner to produce a PUT URL for a specific key valid for a few minutes; the client uploads the bytes straight to S3 with that URL; S3 verifies the signature and stores the object. For downloads you mint a GET URL the same way. Your API handles only tiny JSON, never the file. In code the generation is `s3Presigner.presignPutObject(req -> req.signatureDuration(Duration.ofMinutes(5)).putObjectRequest(por))` which returns the signed URL string.

How multi-gigabyte multipart upload works. A single PUT is impractical for very large files because a network blip restarts the whole transfer. S3 multipart upload breaks the object into parts, typically 5 MB to 100 MB each. The flow is: initiate a multipart upload and get an upload ID; for each part, the client (via a presigned URL per part) uploads that chunk and receives an ETag; after all parts are uploaded, the client calls complete with the list of part numbers and ETags, and S3 assembles the final object. Parts upload in parallel for speed, a failed part retries alone, and you can abort to clean up incomplete uploads. This gives resumability, parallelism, and bounded memory per part.

Why you must validate actual MIME type and size, not the extension. The file extension and the client-declared Content-Type are attacker-controlled strings. An attacker renames malware.exe to invoice.pdf and sets Content-Type to application/pdf. If you trust that, you store and later serve an executable as a PDF. The reliable check is the magic bytes, the first few bytes of the file that identify the real format: a PDF starts with the bytes for "%PDF", a PNG starts with a specific 8-byte signature, a JPEG with FF D8 FF. You read the leading bytes and verify they match an allowed type. Libraries like Apache Tika do this detection robustly. You also enforce a hard maximum size before issuing a URL and, for multipart, cap total size, so nobody uploads a 500 GB file to exhaust your storage budget or trigger a cost attack.

Why virus-scan untrusted content. Users upload arbitrary bytes. Those bytes may be malware, and if your system later serves them to other users or opens them in a processing pipeline, you spread infection. So uploaded content lands in a quarantine area, an asynchronous scanner such as ClamAV checks it, and only clean files are promoted to the usable bucket. Infected files are rejected and the user notified. Scanning is asynchronous so it never blocks the upload path.

The senior nuance is that signed URLs must be short-lived and tightly scoped. A URL valid for days or for a whole bucket is a leaked-credential waiting to happen. You scope it to one key, one method, a short expiry, and ideally with a content-length-range and content-type condition so the client cannot upload something other than what you authorized.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India accepts loan documents and KYC videos from customers like Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001). Some are 3 GB scanned archives.

Problem 1 — the app server fell over as a byte pipe. The old design streamed every upload through the service to disk, then to S3. During a loan drive the disk filled and the thread pool drained while the CPU sat idle, because the server was just copying bytes. This is why we mint a presigned URL and let the client upload straight to S3: the server stops being a byte pipe.

Problem 2 — a 3 GB upload kept failing near the end and restarting from zero. A single PUT over a flaky connection never completed. This is why multi-gigabyte files use multipart upload: the file is split into parts, each uploaded and retried independently, and only the failed part is re-sent.

Problem 3 — an attacker uploaded a program renamed to statement.pdf. The old system trusted the .pdf extension and stored it. This is why we verify magic bytes (a real PDF begins with %PDF), enforce a size cap, and virus-scan in quarantine before promoting the file.

The mini-project builds a runnable demo of the control logic: a `PresignService` that mints scoped short-lived URLs, a `MultipartCoordinator` that initiates, tracks parts, and completes a multi-GB upload, a `MagicByteValidator` that checks real file type, a size guard, and a `QuarantineScanner`. It presigns Rajesh's single PDF, runs Priya's 3 GB multipart upload, and rejects a spoofed file.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's 20 MB PDF, Priya's 3 GB video, a spoofed EXE named statement.pdf, and a genuine PDF.

Step 1: Rajesh's 20 MB is under the 100 MB single-PUT limit, so SizeGuard passes it. PresignService mints a PUT URL for key SAV2001/loan_form.pdf valid five minutes. Rajesh uploads the bytes directly to S3; the server never sees them.

Step 2: Priya's 3 GB exceeds the single-PUT limit, so it goes multipart. The coordinator initiates and gets an upload ID. planParts divides 3 GB by 16 MB parts, giving 192 parts.

Step 3: For each part the coordinator mints a per-part presigned URL. Priya's client uploads each 16 MB chunk directly to S3 and collects an ETag per part. A failed part retries alone, not the whole 3 GB.

Step 4: After all 192 parts are in, complete is called with the part numbers and ETags, and S3 assembles the final object. Priya's video exists as one object.

Step 5: The spoofed file arrives with extension .pdf and declared type application/pdf, but its first bytes are MZ, the DOS executable header. MagicByteValidator detects application/x-dosexec, which is not in the allowed set, and throws UnsupportedFileTypeException. The spoof is rejected regardless of its fake label.

Step 6: The genuine PDF begins with %PDF, so the validator detects application/pdf and passes it. It lands in quarantine, the scanner checks it, returns CLEAN, and it is promoted to the clean bucket for use.

  │    validates, Scanner scans — each one job               │

  │ D: coordinator depends on PresignService abstraction     │

  │  PresignService  │◀──────│ MultipartCoordinator  │
  │ + presignPut()   │        │ - partSize: long      │

  │  SizeGuard   │  │ MagicByteValidator│ │ QuarantineScanner│
  │+ checkSingle │  │ + validate()      │ │ + scan(key)      │
  │+ checkTotal  │  │ - detect(bytes)   │ └──────────────────┘
  └──────────────┘  └──────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Multipart Upload ────────────────────────

  [INITIATED] ──upload parts──→ [PARTS_UPLOADED] ──complete──→ [ASSEMBLED]
       │                              │
       │ abort / timeout              │ part fails → retry that part only
       ▼                              └──────────────┐
  [ABORTED] (S3 cleans incomplete parts)             ▼
                                              (stays PARTS_UPLOADED)

  ── State Diagram: File Trust ──────────────────────────────

  [UPLOADED→quarantine] ──magic ok + scan clean──→ [PROMOTED clean]
          │ magic bad                    │ infected
          ▼                              ▼

  ── Call Chain (Priya 3GB) ─────────────────────────────────

  1. checkTotal(3GB) ≤ 5GB cap → ok
  2. initiate(CUR3001, kyc_video.mp4) → uploadId

sections.s6_takeaway:
I do not route uploaded file bytes through my application server because doing so couples three scarce resources to the size and duration of every upload: heap memory if I buffer, a request thread held for the entire transfer, and local disk if I spool to temp files. A single slow multi-gigabyte upload on a mobile connection can hold a thread for ten minutes, and a few hundred concurrent large uploads exhaust the thread pool, blow the heap, or fill the disk, while the CPU sits idle because the server is doing no real work, just copying bytes. The application server should spend its threads on business logic, not on being a dumb byte pipe that object storage does far better and cheaper.

Instead I use presigned URLs. Object storage like S3 can generate a URL that embeds a signature derived from my backend credentials, the specific bucket and key, the allowed method, and a short expiry. The client asks my API to upload, I authenticate and validate the request and mint a PUT URL valid for a few minutes, and the client then uploads the bytes directly to S3 using that URL while my API only ever handles tiny JSON. For downloads I mint a GET URL the same way. The key safety rule is that the URL must be short-lived and tightly scoped to one key and one operation, ideally with a content-length-range condition, so a leaked URL expires quickly and cannot be abused.

For multi-gigabyte files a single PUT is impractical because any network blip restarts the whole transfer, so I use S3 multipart upload. I initiate and get an upload ID, the client uploads each part through its own presigned URL and collects an ETag per part, parts upload in parallel and a failed part retries on its own, and finally a complete call with the list of part numbers and ETags tells S3 to assemble the object. This gives me parallelism, resumability, and bounded memory per part, which is exactly how we fixed Priya's 3 GB KYC video that previously failed near the end and restarted from zero.

On validation, I never trust the file extension or the client-declared content type, because both are attacker-controlled strings. An attacker renames an executable to statement.pdf and claims it is a PDF. So I read the file's magic bytes, the leading signature that identifies the real format, where a PDF begins with the bytes for percent-P-D-F and an executable begins with MZ, and I reject anything whose real type is not in my allow-list. I enforce a hard maximum size before issuing any URL so nobody can trigger a storage or cost attack, and because users upload arbitrary untrusted bytes, uploaded content lands in a quarantine bucket where an asynchronous scanner like ClamAV checks it, and only clean files are promoted to the usable bucket while infected files are deleted and the user alerted.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that my API mints a short-lived, scoped, signed URL and then steps aside, so bytes travel directly from the client to object storage, very large files go up as independently retryable multipart chunks, and I trust the file's actual magic bytes and enforce a size cap and a quarantine virus scan rather than ever trusting its extension or declared type.

answers.question: Why does a Spring Boot `MultipartFile` upload fail once the file exceeds ~1–10 MB (`MaxUploadSizeExceededException` / `SizeLimitExceededException`), what are the default limits (`spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size` ≈ 1MB and `max-request-size` ≈ 10MB), how do you raise them (those properties, or a programmatic `MultipartConfigElement`/`MultipartConfigFactory`), and why is simply raising the limit the WRONG answer for truly large uploads — stream the `InputStream` instead of buffering the whole file in memory (to avoid OOM), and prefer direct-to-object-storage (presigned URL) or chunked uploads?
answers.shortTitle: Why does a Spring Boot MultipartFile upload fail past a few MB, what are the default limits, how do you raise them, and why is raising the limit the wrong fix for truly large uploads

s1_definition.profdef: Spring Boot applies two multipart limits by default, `spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size` at about 1 MB per file and `spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size` at about 10 MB for the whole request, and exceeding them throws `MaxUploadSizeExceededException` (wrapping the servlet container's `SizeLimitExceededException`). You raise them with those properties or programmatically via a `MultipartConfigElement` built from a `MultipartConfigFactory`. But raising the number is the wrong answer for genuinely large files, because `MultipartFile.getBytes()` buffers the entire file in heap, so large uploads cause OutOfMemoryError under concurrency. The correct approach is to stream the file's `InputStream` to its destination without buffering, and for very large files to bypass the application server entirely using presigned direct-to-object-storage uploads or chunked uploads.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India's online form has a small letterbox slot, big enough for a one-page form (1 MB) and a whole envelope of pages (10 MB total). When Rajesh tries to post a thick 50 MB loan file, it does not fit and gets rejected with a "too large" notice. You can widen the slot (raise the limits), but if you make it huge and a thousand customers all shove thick files through at once, the mailroom floor (heap memory) is buried under piles of paper and the whole branch collapses. The real fix is not a bigger slot but a conveyor belt that carries each page straight to the warehouse as it arrives (streaming), or better, giving customers a gate pass to deliver straight to the warehouse themselves (presigned URL).
s1_definition.oneliner: Defaults are ~1 MB per file and ~10 MB per request; raise them with properties for modestly larger files, but for truly large files stream the InputStream or go direct-to-storage, because getBytes buffers the whole file in the heap.

sections.s2_technical:
Why it fails. When a browser or client posts `multipart/form-data`, the servlet container (Tomcat under Spring Boot) parses the parts. Spring Boot's autoconfiguration sets guardrails so a single huge or malicious upload cannot exhaust server resources by default. The two limits are `max-file-size`, the maximum size of any one uploaded file, defaulting to roughly 1 MB, and `max-request-size`, the maximum size of the entire multipart request including all files and form fields, defaulting to roughly 10 MB. When an upload exceeds either, Spring throws `MaxUploadSizeExceededException`, which wraps the container's `SizeLimitExceededException` or `FileSizeLimitExceededException`. If you do not handle it, the client gets an ugly 500; you should catch it in a `@ControllerAdvice` and return a clean 413 Payload Too Large.

How to raise the limits with properties. In `application.yml` you set:

```yaml
spring:
  servlet:
    multipart:
      max-file-size: 50MB
      max-request-size: 60MB
```

This lets a 50 MB file through, with a little headroom in the request size for form fields and boundaries.

How to raise them programmatically. Sometimes you need to compute limits at runtime or you are not using the property path. You define a `MultipartConfigElement` bean built from `MultipartConfigFactory`:

```java
@Bean
public MultipartConfigElement multipartConfigElement() {
    MultipartConfigFactory factory = new MultipartConfigFactory();
    factory.setMaxFileSize(DataSize.ofMegabytes(50));
    factory.setMaxRequestSize(DataSize.ofMegabytes(60));
    factory.setFileSizeThreshold(DataSize.ofKilobytes(256)); // spill to disk above this
    return factory.createMultipartConfig();
}
```

The `fileSizeThreshold` is important: below it, the part is kept in memory; above it, the container spills the part to a temp file on disk instead of holding it in the heap. Raising the threshold too high reintroduces the memory problem.

Why raising the limit is the wrong answer for truly large files. The tempting fix is to set `max-file-size: 5GB` and move on. But the real danger is how the file is consumed. If your controller does `byte[] data = file.getBytes();` or `file.getBumptedContent()` style, you load the entire file into the heap as a byte array. A 5 GB file is 5 GB of heap for one request; a handful of concurrent large uploads is an instant OutOfMemoryError that crashes the whole JVM, taking down every other user's request with it. So the limit is not the real constraint, memory is. Raising the limit without changing how you read the file just converts a clean 413 rejection into a catastrophic OOM crash.

The correct approach when the file must pass through your service: stream the `InputStream`. Instead of `getBytes()`, you call `file.getInputStream()` and copy it in fixed-size chunks to the destination, such as `StreamUtils.copy(in, out)` or `Files.copy(in, targetPath)`, or pipe it to an S3 `PutObjectRequest` using `RequestBody.fromInputStream(in, contentLength)`. Only one chunk is in memory at a time, so memory stays bounded no matter how large the file or how many concurrent uploads. You still cap total size to prevent abuse, but you do it with a streaming-aware guard, not by buffering.

The best approach for genuinely large files: do not pass bytes through your service at all. Use presigned URLs so the client uploads directly to object storage, or chunked/multipart uploads for multi-gigabyte files. Then the `max-file-size` property is irrelevant because the file never becomes a `MultipartFile` on your server; your API only handles small control requests. This is the architecture that actually scales.

The senior nuance is matching the tool to the size. For small files like a profile photo or a one-page PDF, a `MultipartFile` with a modestly raised limit and streamed `getInputStream()` is perfectly fine and simplest. For tens or hundreds of megabytes, stream and consider WebFlux for concurrency. For gigabytes, always go direct-to-storage with presigned multipart. Blindly raising the limit on a buffering controller is the anti-pattern.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India lets customers upload supporting documents. Rajesh (SAV2001) uploads a 40 MB scanned loan packet; the online portal serves thousands of customers during a loan campaign.

Problem 1 — the upload failed at 1 MB with a confusing 500 error. The default `max-file-size` of 1 MB rejected Rajesh's 40 MB file, and the uncaught `MaxUploadSizeExceededException` gave him a stack trace instead of a clear message. This is why we raise the limit sensibly and handle the exception to return a clean 413.

Problem 2 — after raising the limit to 5 GB, the server crashed with OutOfMemoryError. The controller read the whole file into a byte array with getBytes, so a few hundred concurrent 40 MB uploads buried the heap. This is why we must stream the InputStream instead of buffering, so memory stays bounded.

Problem 3 — even streaming, a customer's 3 GB archive still tied up a thread for minutes and risked disk fill. This is why truly large files should bypass the service with a presigned direct-to-storage upload.

The mini-project builds a runnable demo of the decision logic and streaming copy: a `MultipartLimits` holder, a `MultipartExceptionHandler` mapping to 413, an `UploadHandler` that streams small/medium files chunk-by-chunk (bounded memory) and routes large files to presigned direct upload. It processes a 40 MB streamed upload and a 3 GB direct-upload routing decision, and shows the 413 path for a file over the cap.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's 40 MB PDF, Priya's 3 GB archive, and a 6 GB file.

Step 1: Rajesh's 40 MB enters the handler. It is under the 5 GB absolute cap and under the 50 MB direct-upload threshold, so it takes the streaming path.

Step 2: streamToStorage reads the InputStream in 8 KB chunks and writes each chunk to storage before reading the next. At any instant only 8 KB is in memory, so even with hundreds of concurrent 40 MB uploads the heap stays tiny. The outcome is STREAMED.

Step 3: Priya's 3 GB enters the handler. It is under the 5 GB cap but over the 50 MB direct threshold, so instead of passing bytes through the server the handler mints a presigned URL and returns DIRECT_PRESIGNED. Priya's client will upload straight to S3; the server never touches the 3 GB.

Step 4: The 6 GB file enters. It exceeds the 5 GB absolute cap, so the handler throws PayloadTooLargeException before doing any work. In the real service the @ControllerAdvice turns this into a clean HTTP 413 rather than a 500 stack trace.

Step 5: Contrast with the broken approach: had the controller called getBytes on Priya's 3 GB, the heap would have tried to allocate a 3 GB byte array, and a few concurrent such uploads would have thrown OutOfMemoryError and crashed the JVM for everyone. Streaming and direct-upload both avoid that.

2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] Priya outcome: DIRECT_PRESIGNED — client uploads straight to S3: https://nbi-docs.s3.amazonaws.com/CUR3001/archive.zip?X-Amz-Signature=SIM

answers.question: Write Redis-based distributed lock logic for a scheduled task (`setIfAbsent` with TTL).
answers.shortTitle: Write Redis-based distributed lock logic for a scheduled task

s1_definition.profdef: A Redis distributed lock lets multiple instances of a service agree that only one of them runs a critical section at a time. It is implemented with an atomic `SET key value NX PX ttl` (exposed in Spring as `opsForValue().setIfAbsent(key, token, ttl)`), which succeeds only if the key does not already exist and auto-expires after the TTL so a crashed holder never deadlocks the system. The lock value is a unique token so that only the owner can release it, and release is done with a Lua script that checks the token before deleting, making check-and-delete atomic. For scheduled tasks across a horizontally scaled deployment, this guarantees the job fires once per schedule, not once per instance.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India runs the nightly interest calculation. The service runs on five servers for high availability, so at 2 AM all five wake up and all five try to calculate interest for Rajesh and Priya, which would credit interest five times. To prevent that, there is a single key hanging on a hook in a shared room (Redis). The rule: whoever grabs the key first does the job, and everyone else sees the hook is empty and quietly goes back to sleep. The key is tagged with the name of who took it, so only that person can return it. And the key automatically falls back on the hook after a set time, so if the holder faints mid-job, the key is not lost forever.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use SET NX PX (setIfAbsent with TTL) so only one instance acquires the lock, the TTL prevents deadlock on crash, and a token-checked Lua release ensures only the owner unlocks.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Redis distributed lock lets multiple instances of a service agree that only one of them runs a critical section at a time. It is implemented with an atomic `SET key value NX PX ttl` (exposed in Spring as `opsForValue().setIfAbsent(key, token, ttl)`), which succeeds only if the key does not already exist and auto-expires after the TTL so a crashed holder never deadlocks the system. The lock value is a unique token so that only the owner can release it, and release is done with a Lua script that checks the token before deleting, making check-and-delete atomic. For scheduled tasks across a horizontally scaled deployment, this guarantees the job fires once per schedule, not once per instance.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India runs the nightly interest calculation. The service runs on five servers for high availability, so at 2 AM all five wake up and all five try to calculate interest for Rajesh and Priya, which would credit interest five times. To prevent that, there is a single key hanging on a hook in a shared room (Redis). The rule: whoever grabs the key first does the job, and everyone else sees the hook is empty and quietly goes back to sleep. The key is tagged with the name of who took it, so only that person can return it. And the key automatically falls back on the hook after a set time, so if the holder faints mid-job, the key is not lost forever.

**One line to remember:** Use SET NX PX (setIfAbsent with TTL) so only one instance acquires the lock, the TTL prevents deadlock on crash, and a token-checked Lua release ensures only the owner unlocks.

sections.s2_technical:
The problem it solves. When you scale a service horizontally for availability, every instance has the same scheduled job. Without coordination, a cron at 2 AM fires on all five instances and the interest posting runs five times. You need mutual exclusion across machines, which a local Java lock cannot provide because each JVM has its own lock object. Redis, being a single shared fast store, becomes the coordination point.

Why setIfAbsent with TTL. The core operation is Redis `SET key value NX PX milliseconds`. NX means "only set if the key does not already exist," which is atomic, so exactly one of the racing instances wins. PX sets an expiry in milliseconds. In Spring Data Redis this is `redisTemplate.opsForValue().setIfAbsent("lock:interest-posting", token, Duration.ofSeconds(60))`, which returns true to the one winner and false to everyone else. The winner runs the job; the losers skip.

Why a TTL is mandatory. Suppose the winner acquires the lock and then its JVM crashes or the machine dies before releasing. Without a TTL the lock key stays forever and the job never runs again on any instance, a permanent deadlock. The TTL is a safety valve: the lock auto-expires, so the next scheduled run can acquire it. You set the TTL comfortably longer than the worst-case job duration so the lock does not expire while the job is still running.

Why a unique token. The lock value must be a unique identifier for this acquisition, such as a UUID or instance-id plus timestamp. This prevents the classic wrong-release bug: instance A acquires the lock, the job runs long and the TTL expires, Redis frees the lock, instance B acquires it, and then instance A finishes and blindly deletes the lock, but it just deleted B's lock. By storing a unique token and releasing only if the stored token equals mine, A sees the token no longer matches and does not delete B's lock.

Why release must be atomic with a Lua script. Releasing naively is "GET the key, if it equals my token then DEL it." But between the GET and the DEL, the TTL could expire and another instance could acquire, so you would delete their lock. Redis solves this by running a small Lua script atomically on the server: `if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end`. The check and delete happen as one indivisible operation, so you only ever delete your own lock.

Handling long-running jobs with a watchdog. If a job might run longer than the TTL, you either set a generous TTL or run a background watchdog that periodically extends the TTL (also via a token-checked Lua script that calls PEXPIRE only if the token matches) while the job is still alive. This is what libraries like Redisson do automatically with lock leases.

When to use a library versus hand-rolling. For a simple scheduled-task guard, hand-rolled setIfAbsent plus Lua release is perfectly fine and easy to reason about. For stronger guarantees across Redis failover you can use Redisson, which implements the Redlock algorithm, lock leasing, watchdog renewal, and reentrancy. The senior nuance is honesty about guarantees: a single-Redis lock is not a perfect distributed lock under network partitions and failover; it is a practical "mostly once" guard that, combined with an idempotent job, is correct in practice. For money-critical jobs you also make the job itself idempotent so that even a rare double-run does not double-post.

The combination to remember is lock plus idempotency. The lock makes double execution rare; idempotency makes it harmless if it ever happens.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India posts daily interest to savings accounts. The posting service runs on multiple instances for high availability, and a scheduled job fires every night.

Problem 1 — interest was posted multiple times. All three instances fired the job at 2 AM and each credited Rajesh's savings account, tripling his interest. This is why we need a distributed lock so only one instance actually runs the posting.

Problem 2 — one night a lock was taken and the instance crashed, and the job never ran again. The lock key was stuck with no expiry. This is why the lock must have a TTL that auto-expires, so the next night can acquire it.

Problem 3 — a long run expired its own lock and a second instance started, then the first instance finished and deleted the second's lock. This is why the lock value is a unique token and release is a token-checked atomic Lua script, so an instance only ever releases its own lock.

The mini-project builds a runnable demo of the lock logic: a `DistributedLock` abstraction with acquire (setIfAbsent with TTL and unique token) and release (token-checked atomic delete), a simulated `FakeRedis` that is thread-safe, and an `InterestPostingJob` guarded by the lock. Three threads simulate three instances racing to run the nightly job; only one succeeds, and the job is also idempotent as a safety net.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three instances fire the nightly job at the same instant. Rajesh starts at 1,000,000 and Priya at 250,000.

Step 1: All three threads reach runNightly and call tryAcquire almost simultaneously. Each generates its own unique token.

Step 2: Each calls setIfAbsent on the same key. FakeRedis is synchronized, so the calls serialize. The first thread finds the key absent and sets it with its token and a 120-second TTL, returning true. The other two find the key present and not expired, so NX fails and they get false.

Step 3: Instance-2 (say the winner) gets a non-null token and logs ACQUIRED. Instances 1 and 3 get null and log that they skipped. Only one instance will post interest.

Step 4: The winner iterates accounts. Rajesh's daily interest is 1,000,000 times the daily rate, rounded to 109.60, credited once. Priya's is credited once. Balances update exactly once.

Step 5: In the finally block the winner calls release with its token. compareAndDelete finds the stored token equals the winner's token and deletes the key. If the losers had somehow called release, their token would not match and nothing would be deleted, protecting the owner's lock.

Step 6: Because the TTL also exists, even if the winner had crashed before releasing, the key would expire after 120 seconds and the next scheduled run could acquire it. No permanent deadlock.

Final output:

```

2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] instance-1 did NOT get the lock — skipping (another instance is posting)

Note the interest was credited exactly once, not three times.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Redis distributed lock lets me guarantee that a scheduled job runs once per schedule rather than once per instance, which matters the moment I scale a service horizontally for availability, because then the same cron fires on every instance. On my project at National Bank of India the nightly interest posting ran on three instances, and without coordination all three credited Rajesh and Priya, tripling their interest. A local Java lock cannot fix this because each JVM has its own lock object, so I need a shared coordination point, and Redis is a fast single store that serves that role perfectly.

The core of the lock is the atomic SET key value NX PX operation, which in Spring Data Redis is opsForValue().setIfAbsent with a TTL. NX means set only if the key does not already exist, so when all three instances race, Redis guarantees exactly one wins and gets true while the others get false, and only the winner runs the job. The TTL is mandatory for safety: if the winner crashes after acquiring but before releasing, without a TTL the lock would stay forever and the job would never run again, a permanent deadlock, so the TTL auto-expires the lock and lets the next scheduled run acquire it. I set the TTL comfortably longer than the worst-case job duration.

Two subtle correctness points matter. First, the lock value must be a unique token like a UUID, not a constant, because of the wrong-release bug: if instance A's job runs past the TTL, Redis frees the lock, instance B acquires it, and then A finishes and blindly deletes the lock, it would delete B's lock. By storing a unique token and releasing only when the stored token still equals mine, A sees the mismatch and leaves B's lock alone. Second, the release must be atomic, so I use a small Lua script that reads the value and deletes it only if it equals my token in a single indivisible server-side operation, because a naive GET-then-DEL has a race between the two steps. For jobs that might outlast the TTL I either set a generous TTL or run a watchdog that extends it, which is what Redisson does automatically.

I am also honest about the guarantees. A single-Redis lock is a practical mostly-once guard, not a perfect distributed lock under network partitions and Redis failover, so for money-critical jobs I combine the lock with an idempotent job, for example a posting-date marker so that even a rare double-run does not double-post interest. The lock makes double execution rare and idempotency makes it harmless if it ever happens, and together they are correct in practice.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I acquire with setIfAbsent using NX plus a TTL so exactly one instance wins and a crash cannot deadlock, I store a unique token and release it with a token-checked atomic Lua script so I only ever unlock my own lock, and I back the lock with an idempotent job so the scheduled task is effectively run-once even across a horizontally scaled, highly available deployment.

answers.question: Implement a simple round-robin load balancer in Java (`AtomicInteger`).
answers.shortTitle: Implement a simple round-robin load balancer in Java using AtomicInteger

s1_definition.profdef: A round-robin load balancer distributes incoming requests evenly across a list of backend servers by cycling through them in order, server 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, and so on. In Java the thread-safe way to pick the next index without locks is an `AtomicInteger` whose `getAndIncrement` is atomically mapped onto the server list with a modulo, so concurrent threads each get a distinct, monotonically advancing counter value and no two threads collide on the same tick. For a production-grade balancer you also guard against unbounded counter growth, skip unhealthy nodes, and optionally weight servers by capacity.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India has five teller counters serving customers like Rajesh and Priya. A round-robin host at the door sends the first customer to counter 1, the next to counter 2, and so on, looping back to counter 1 after counter 5, so every counter gets a fair, equal share and none is overwhelmed while others sit idle. The host keeps a single tally counter, and because many customers arrive at once, the tally must be updated atomically so two customers are never sent to the same counter by mistake and the count never gets corrupted.
s1_definition.oneliner: Round-robin cycles backends in order; an AtomicInteger's getAndIncrement modulo the server count gives a lock-free, thread-safe next pick.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A round-robin load balancer distributes incoming requests evenly across a list of backend servers by cycling through them in order, server 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, and so on. In Java the thread-safe way to pick the next index without locks is an `AtomicInteger` whose `getAndIncrement` is atomically mapped onto the server list with a modulo, so concurrent threads each get a distinct, monotonically advancing counter value and no two threads collide on the same tick. For a production-grade balancer you also guard against unbounded counter growth, skip unhealthy nodes, and optionally weight servers by capacity.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India has five teller counters serving customers like Rajesh and Priya. A round-robin host at the door sends the first customer to counter 1, the next to counter 2, and so on, looping back to counter 1 after counter 5, so every counter gets a fair, equal share and none is overwhelmed while others sit idle. The host keeps a single tally counter, and because many customers arrive at once, the tally must be updated atomically so two customers are never sent to the same counter by mistake and the count never gets corrupted.

**One line to remember:** Round-robin cycles backends in order; an AtomicInteger's getAndIncrement modulo the server count gives a lock-free, thread-safe next pick.

sections.s2_technical:
The core idea. Given a list of N backends, request number k goes to backend `k % N`. The only shared state is the counter k. If you used a plain `int` and did `index = counter++`, that is not thread-safe: under concurrency two threads can read the same value before either writes back, so they both pick the same backend and the distribution skews. You need the increment to be atomic.

Why AtomicInteger. `AtomicInteger.getAndIncrement()` performs a read-modify-write as one indivisible hardware-level compare-and-swap operation, so every concurrent caller receives a distinct value and the counter advances exactly once per call. You then map that value onto the list with modulo: `int index = Math.floorMod(counter.getAndIncrement(), servers.size())`. floorMod is used instead of the plain `%` operator because when the int counter eventually overflows past Integer.MAX_VALUE it wraps to a negative number, and `%` would then produce a negative index that throws IndexOutOfBoundsException, whereas floorMod always returns a non-negative result in the range 0 to N-1.

Handling counter overflow. Over billions of requests the AtomicInteger will overflow. Using floorMod keeps the index valid even after the wrap, so correctness is preserved. Alternatively you can periodically reset or mask the counter, but floorMod is the simplest correct approach and is what I prefer.

Health checks and skipping dead nodes. A naive round-robin keeps sending traffic to a server that is down. A real balancer tracks each backend's health and, when it lands on an unhealthy one, advances to the next healthy one. You maintain a health flag per backend, updated by a background health-check pinger, and the pick loop skips unhealthy nodes, falling back gracefully if all are down.

Weighted round-robin. Not all servers are equal; a bigger instance can take more traffic. Weighted round-robin assigns each backend a weight and distributes proportionally, for example a weight-3 server gets three times the traffic of a weight-1 server. A simple implementation expands the list so a weight-3 server appears three times, or uses a smooth weighted algorithm that interleaves them to avoid bursts to one node.

Why this matters versus alternatives. Round-robin is stateless per request and gives even distribution when requests are roughly equal in cost, which is its strength and its weakness: if one request is very expensive it still counts as one tick, so round-robin does not account for actual load. Least-connections or least-response-time strategies adapt to real load but need more shared state. Round-robin's simplicity and the lock-free AtomicInteger make it extremely fast and contention-light, which is why it is a common default.

The senior nuance is contention. Under very high throughput even a single AtomicInteger can become a contention hotspot because every thread hits the same cache line. For extreme scale you can shard the counter or use a `LongAdder`-style striped counter, trading perfect ordering for throughput, since round-robin does not actually require globally perfect ordering, only roughly even distribution. For the vast majority of services a single AtomicInteger is more than fast enough.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India's transfer API runs on multiple backend instances. A client-side load balancer in the gateway spreads incoming transfer requests across those instances.

Problem 1 — traffic was skewed to one instance. The first version used a plain int counter incremented without synchronization, so under load several threads read the same counter value and routed to the same backend, overloading it while others idled. This is why the next-index pick must use an AtomicInteger so every concurrent request gets a distinct tick.

Problem 2 — requests were sent to a crashed instance. When one backend died, round-robin kept sending every third request to it, and those requests failed. This is why the balancer must track health and skip unhealthy backends.

Problem 3 — a larger instance was underused. One backend had double the CPU but got the same share as the small ones. This is why we support weighted round-robin so the big instance takes proportionally more traffic.

The mini-project builds a runnable demo: a `Backend` with an address and health flag, a `RoundRobinLoadBalancer` using an AtomicInteger with floorMod that skips unhealthy nodes, and a `WeightedRoundRobinLoadBalancer`. It routes a burst of concurrent transfer requests for Rajesh and Priya, shows even distribution, shows skipping a downed node, and shows weighting.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three backends svc-1 (weight 1), svc-2 (weight 1), svc-3 (weight 2), and bursts of concurrent requests.

Step 1: Nine requests fire concurrently and each calls next. Each thread calls counter.getAndIncrement, which atomically hands out distinct values 0 through 8. No two threads get the same value, so no two collide on the same backend by accident.

Step 2: Each value is mapped with floorMod over size 3, producing indices 0,1,2,0,1,2,0,1,2. Over nine requests each of the three backends is picked exactly three times, an even distribution.

Step 3: svc-2 is marked unhealthy. Now six requests come in. Each call lands on an index via getAndIncrement; when it lands on svc-2 the health check fails, so the loop advances to the next index and returns a healthy backend. svc-2 receives zero requests; svc-1 and svc-3 share them.

Step 4: For weighted round-robin, the expanded list is [svc-1, svc-2, svc-3, svc-3] because svc-3 has weight 2 and appears twice. Eight requests cycle over this length-4 list twice, so svc-1 gets 2, svc-2 gets 2, and svc-3 gets 4, exactly double the others.

Step 5: Over billions of requests the AtomicInteger would overflow past Integer.MAX_VALUE into negatives, but floorMod still returns a valid non-negative index, so routing stays correct forever.

  │RoundRobinLB      │  │WeightedRoundRobinLB       │
  │- counter:Atomic  │  │- expanded: List<Backend>  │
  │- backends:List   │  │- counter: AtomicInteger   │
  │+ next()          │  │+ next()                   │
  └────────┬─────────┘  └────────┬──────────────────┘
           │ holds               │ holds
           ▼                     ▼
       ┌──────────────┐
       │   Backend    │
       │ address      │
       │ weight       │
       │ healthy (vol)│◀── HealthChecker.check()
       └──────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Backend Health ──────────────────────────

  [HEALTHY] ──ping fails──→ [UNHEALTHY] ──ping ok──→ [HEALTHY]
     (routed to)              (skipped by next())

  ── Call Chain (9 concurrent requests) ─────────────────────

  1. thread-k → next()
  2.   tick = counter.getAndIncrement()   (atomic, distinct)
  3.   index = floorMod(tick, 3)
  4.   backend = backends.get(index)
  5.   healthy? return : advance to next index
  → svc-1 ×3, svc-2 ×3, svc-3 ×3
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A round-robin load balancer distributes requests evenly across a list of backends by cycling through them in order, so request k goes to backend k modulo N. The only shared state is the counter, and that is exactly where thread safety matters. If I use a plain int and do index equals counter plus plus, that is not atomic: under concurrency two threads can read the same value before either writes it back, so they route to the same backend and the distribution skews, which is a bug we actually hit when one instance got overloaded while others sat idle. The fix is an AtomicInteger, whose getAndIncrement is a single indivisible compare-and-swap, so every concurrent caller receives a distinct, monotonically advancing value and no two collide.

I map that counter onto the backend list with Math.floorMod rather than the plain percent operator. This is a detail I always mention: over billions of requests the int counter overflows past Integer.MAX_VALUE and wraps to a negative number, and the percent operator would then produce a negative index that throws IndexOutOfBoundsException, whereas floorMod always returns a non-negative result in the valid range, so routing stays correct forever even after the overflow. This gives a completely lock-free next-pick that is extremely fast and contention-light.

A production balancer does more than cycle blindly. It tracks each backend's health with a flag updated by a background health-check pinger, and when the pick lands on an unhealthy node it advances to the next healthy one, which is how I fixed requests being sent to a crashed instance. It also supports weighted round-robin for unequal instances: a bigger server gets a larger weight and proportionally more traffic, which I implement simply by expanding the list so a weight-two server appears twice and then round-robining over the expanded list with the same AtomicInteger trick. Over eight requests, a weight-two backend among three then receives four while the others receive two each.

I am also aware of the trade-offs. Round-robin treats every request as one equal tick, so it does not account for a single very expensive request, which is where least-connections or least-response-time strategies adapt better at the cost of more shared state. And at extreme throughput even one AtomicInteger can become a cache-line contention hotspot, in which case I would shard the counter or use a striped counter, because round-robin only needs roughly even distribution, not globally perfect ordering. For the vast majority of services a single AtomicInteger with floorMod and health-aware skipping is more than fast enough.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I implement round-robin with an AtomicInteger whose getAndIncrement gives each concurrent request a distinct tick, I map it to a backend with floorMod so overflow never breaks the index, and I extend it with health-aware skipping and weighted expansion so the balancer is thread-safe, lock-free, resilient to dead nodes, and fair to unequal instances.
