sections.s2_technical:
In a microservices system, instances come and go constantly — they scale up, scale down, crash, restart, and move hosts — so no caller can hardcode addresses. Service discovery is the mechanism that answers "where are the healthy instances of service X right now." There are two broad styles, and Eureka and Kubernetes represent them.

Eureka implements client-side discovery with a dedicated registry server. The lifecycle has three parts. On startup, each instance registers with Eureka, sending its service name, host, port, and metadata. This creates a lease. To keep the lease alive, the instance sends a heartbeat on a fixed interval, by default every thirty seconds; each heartbeat renews the lease. If Eureka does not receive heartbeats within the lease-expiration window, it evicts that instance from the registry, so stale or dead instances fall out automatically. On the client side, callers fetch the registry — typically caching it locally and refreshing periodically — and then pick an instance using a client-side load balancer. The client, not a central proxy, decides which instance to call.

```java
// Eureka client-side discovery (conceptual): fetch instances, load-balance locally
List<InstanceInfo> instances = eurekaClient.getInstancesByServiceName("transfer-service");
InstanceInfo chosen = clientLoadBalancer.choose(instances); // client decides
String url = "http://" + chosen.getIPAddr() + ":" + chosen.getPort() + "/api/v1/transfers";
```

A notable property of Eureka is that it deliberately favours availability over strict consistency. During a network partition it enters self-preservation mode, keeping registrations it can no longer confirm rather than evicting everything, on the theory that stale-but-maybe-alive entries are safer than an empty registry that makes the whole system undiscoverable. This is an AP choice in CAP terms, appropriate for discovery where a temporarily stale list is better than no list.

Kubernetes-native discovery removes the separate registry application by making discovery a platform responsibility. You declare a Service object that selects a set of pods by label. The platform's endpoint controller continuously tracks which of those pods are ready — using readiness probes — and maintains the Service's endpoint list. CoreDNS, the in-cluster DNS server, resolves the Service's name (for example transfer-service.default.svc.cluster.local) to the Service's stable virtual IP or directly to the ready pod endpoints. A caller simply makes an HTTP request to the service name, DNS resolves it, and kube-proxy or the Service load-balances to a healthy pod. There is no registration library in the application and no heartbeat you write; the application just exposes a readiness endpoint, and the platform does registration, health tracking, eviction, and load balancing.

```yaml
# Kubernetes: the Service IS the discovery mechanism — no Eureka server, no client library
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: transfer-service }
spec:
  selector: { app: transfer }     # platform tracks ready pods with this label
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]
# Caller just does: http://transfer-service/api/v1/transfers  (CoreDNS resolves it)
```

The key differences follow from this. Eureka requires you to run and operate a registry cluster and embed a client library in every service, giving you client-side load balancing and rich metadata, and it works anywhere there is a network. Kubernetes-native discovery requires no extra server or library because the platform owns it, uses DNS plus readiness probes rather than application heartbeats, and typically does server-side or kube-proxy load balancing, but it only works within the Kubernetes world. So the senior-level guidance on when you still need Eureka: when your services are not on Kubernetes at all, for example on virtual machines or bare metal; when you span multiple clouds or hybrid on-premise-plus-cloud environments where no single Kubernetes cluster owns every instance; and during a gradual migration where some services already run on Kubernetes while others do not, and you need one discovery mechanism that spans both until the migration completes. In a greenfield, single-cluster Kubernetes deployment, adding Eureka is usually redundant complexity because the platform already provides discovery; the honest principal-level answer is to use the platform's native mechanism when you are fully on the platform, and reach for an explicit registry like Eureka precisely when you are not, or not yet.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the transfer service needs to call the account service, whose instances scale up and down and occasionally crash. Callers cannot hardcode addresses.

Problem 1 — without discovery, a crashed account instance still receives traffic and transfers fail. The system needs a live directory of healthy instances with automatic eviction of dead ones.

Problem 2 — the bank is partway through moving to Kubernetes: some services are already in a cluster using Services and CoreDNS, while older services still run on virtual machines and need an explicit registry. The design must handle both.

The mini-project simulates a Eureka-style registry with registration, heartbeat leases, and eviction after missed heartbeats, plus client-side lookup and load balancing, and contrasts it with a Kubernetes-style discovery that resolves a service name to ready endpoints with no application heartbeat. The demo registers account instances, shows a client discovering and load-balancing across them, crashes one instance so its lease expires and it is evicted, and then shows the Kubernetes-style resolver returning only ready endpoints without any heartbeat logic in the application.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: two account-service instances register with a Eureka-style registry, a client discovers and load-balances across them, one instance crashes, and then a Kubernetes-style resolver returns ready endpoints.

Step 1 — Instances register. On startup, acct-1 and acct-2 register with the registry, each declaring its service name and address. Each registration creates a lease stamped with the current time. The registry now knows two healthy account instances.

Step 2 — Client discovers and load-balances. The client asks the registry for healthy account-service instances, gets both, and the client-side load balancer picks acct-1 for the first call and acct-2 for the second, round-robin. The client, not a central proxy, chooses the instance.

Step 3 — One instance crashes. acct-1 crashes and stops sending heartbeats. Time advances past the lease-expiration window. acct-2, still alive, sends a heartbeat that renews its lease.

Step 4 — Eviction. The registry runs eviction and finds that acct-1's last heartbeat is older than the lease window, so it evicts acct-1. Now only acct-2 remains healthy. The next client lookup returns just acct-2, so no traffic is sent to the dead instance. The heartbeat lease mechanism removed the dead instance automatically.

Step 5 — Kubernetes-native resolution. For the services already on Kubernetes, there is no registry server and no application heartbeat. The platform's endpoint controller tracks which pods are ready via readiness probes, and CoreDNS resolves the service name account-service to the current ready endpoints. The caller simply makes a request to the name and the platform routes it to a healthy pod. The same outcome — discover healthy instances — is achieved, but the application wrote no registration or heartbeat code at all.

A service registry exists because in a microservices system instances come and go constantly — they scale, crash, restart, and move — so no caller can hardcode addresses, and something has to answer "where are the healthy instances of this service right now." On the client side, callers fetch the registry, cache it, and use a client-side load balancer to pick an instance themselves, so the caller, not a central proxy, decides where the request goes. A characteristic detail is that Eureka favours availability over consistency — during a network partition it enters self-preservation and keeps registrations it cannot confirm, because a stale list is safer for discovery than an empty one.

Kubernetes-native discovery reaches the same outcome but removes the separate registry application by making discovery a platform responsibility. You declare a Service object that selects pods by label, the platform's endpoint controller continuously tracks which of those pods are ready using readiness probes, and CoreDNS, the in-cluster DNS server, resolves the service name to those ready endpoints. A caller just makes an HTTP request to the service name, DNS resolves it, and kube-proxy load-balances to a healthy pod. The crucial difference is that the application writes no registration and no heartbeat code; it only exposes a readiness endpoint, and the platform handles registration, health tracking, eviction, and load balancing. Eureka is a library plus a server you operate with application heartbeats and client-side load balancing; Kubernetes is a built-in capability using DNS and probes with platform-side load balancing.

So the honest answer to when you still need Eureka is that it depends on whether a single platform owns all your instances. If you are fully on a single Kubernetes cluster, adding Eureka is usually redundant complexity, because the platform already provides discovery natively. You still want an explicit registry like Eureka when your services are not on Kubernetes at all — on virtual machines or bare metal — when you span multiple clouds or a hybrid on-premise-plus-cloud estate where no single cluster knows about every instance, and during a gradual migration where some services already run on Kubernetes and others do not, and you need one discovery mechanism that spans both worlds until the migration finishes.

In my banking work this mapped directly onto a migration: older account and transfer services ran on virtual machines and used a Eureka registry with heartbeat leases and client-side load balancing, while newer services ran in a Kubernetes cluster and used Services plus CoreDNS with no discovery code in the application at all. During the transition we kept Eureka as the bridge so both worlds could discover each other, and we retired it for a given service only once that service was fully inside the cluster. The principle I take into interviews is that service discovery is the same problem everywhere — find the healthy instances and route to them — and the right tool is whatever already owns your runtime: the platform's native mechanism when you are on the platform, and an explicit registry like Eureka precisely when you are not, not yet, or spread across several.

answers.question: What is the Raft consensus algorithm — a protocol for achieving agreement across a cluster of nodes on a shared log, using leader election (candidates request votes, majority wins), log replication (the leader appends entries and replicates to followers, committing when a majority acknowledges), and safety (committed entries are never lost even if the leader changes) — and where is it used in practice (etcd for Kubernetes, Consul for service discovery, Kafka KRaft replacing ZooKeeper for metadata consensus)?
answers.shortTitle: What is the Raft consensus algorithm, and where is it used in practice?

s1_definition.profdef: Raft is a consensus algorithm that lets a cluster of nodes agree on a single, consistent, ordered log of commands even when nodes fail or messages are delayed. It works through three mechanisms. Leader election: time is divided into terms, and in each term nodes elect a single leader; a candidate requests votes and becomes leader if it wins a majority. Log replication: all client commands go to the leader, which appends them to its log and replicates them to followers, and an entry is committed once a majority of nodes have stored it. Safety: Raft's voting and commit rules guarantee that a committed entry is never lost and never contradicted, even across leader changes, so every node applies the same commands in the same order. Because commitment requires a majority (a quorum), Raft tolerates the failure of a minority of nodes while remaining correct, which is why it underpins the control planes of etcd (Kubernetes), Consul (service discovery), and Kafka's KRaft metadata layer.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has five branch managers who must all keep an identical master ledger, and no single entry is official until most of them have written it down, so that even if a couple of managers are unreachable, the bank still agrees on what happened. Raft is the rulebook for this. First the managers elect one head manager for the day; whoever gets votes from the majority wins. Then every new ledger entry goes only to the head manager, who writes it and sends copies to the others; the entry becomes official only once more than half the managers have recorded it. And the rules are designed so that once an entry is official, it can never be erased or changed, even if tomorrow a different manager takes over as head. So long as a majority of managers are present, the bank always has one agreed, unchangeable ledger.
s1_definition.oneliner: Raft makes a cluster agree on one ordered log via an elected leader, majority-quorum commits, and safety rules that preserve committed entries across leader changes — and it is the backbone of etcd, Consul, and Kafka KRaft.

sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, a cluster of configuration nodes must agree on a single source of truth for critical settings — for example which data centre is currently the primary for transfers — and this agreement must survive node failures without ever producing two conflicting answers.

Problem 1 — if each node independently decides the primary, a network glitch could leave two nodes both believing they are primary, and transfers could be double-processed. The bank needs exactly one agreed decision at a time.

Problem 2 — the decision must remain correct even if a node crashes, so it cannot depend on any single node; it needs a majority-based agreement that tolerates a minority failing.

The mini-project simulates a small Raft cluster: nodes hold terms and logs, run a leader election requiring a majority of votes, replicate a configuration-change entry from the leader, and commit it only when a majority acknowledge. The demo elects a leader, replicates a "primary = DC1" entry committed by majority, then fails the leader and shows a new leader elected by the remaining majority with the committed entry preserved, demonstrating leader election, majority-commit replication, and safety across a leader change.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a five-node Raft cluster must agree on which data centre is primary, survive the leader crashing, and never lose a committed decision.

Step 1 — Leader election. One node becomes a candidate, increments its term, votes for itself, and requests votes from the others. Each peer grants its vote because the candidate's log is at least as up to date. The candidate collects three votes, which is the majority of five, so it becomes the leader for that term. The cluster now has exactly one leader.

Step 2 — Replicate a configuration entry. A client asks to set the primary to DC1. The leader appends the entry PRIMARY equals DC1 to its own log and sends it to the followers. Five nodes store it, which is well past the majority of three, so the leader marks the entry committed and the followers do too. The decision is now official and identical on every node.

Step 3 — Confirm the commit. The cluster reports that a surviving node holds the committed entry PRIMARY equals DC1 at its log index. This is the single agreed source of truth.

Step 4 — Leader crashes. The leader node fails and stops responding. Because the entry PRIMARY equals DC1 was already committed on a majority, it exists on the surviving four nodes, so the crash cannot erase it. This is the safety guarantee.

Step 5 — Re-election preserves safety. The remaining four nodes, still a majority, elect a new leader. The safety rules ensure the new leader has the committed entry, so after the leader change the committed PRIMARY equals DC1 is still present. The new leader then continues the log by replicating a further entry. Throughout a leader failure, the committed decision was never lost and the cluster never produced two conflicting answers.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Raft is a consensus algorithm that lets a cluster of nodes agree on a single, consistent, ordered log of commands even when some nodes crash or messages are delayed, and it was deliberately designed to be understandable by splitting the problem into three parts: leader election, log replication, and safety. For leader election, Raft divides time into numbered terms, and in each term the nodes elect one leader: a node that stops hearing heartbeats becomes a candidate, increments the term, votes for itself, and requests votes from the others, becoming leader only if it wins a majority. Randomised election timeouts make split votes rare, so the cluster reliably settles on exactly one leader per term.

For log replication, all client commands flow through the leader, which appends each command to its own log and replicates it to the followers with AppendEntries messages, and an entry becomes committed only once a majority of nodes have stored it. Because every node applies committed entries in the same order, all the state machines stay identical. For safety, Raft's rules guarantee that a committed entry is never lost or contradicted even when leaders change: a node only grants its vote to a candidate whose log is at least as up to date, so a node missing committed entries can never win an election; a new leader never deletes committed entries, only brings followers into line; and these rules together ensure every future leader already has every committed entry. The whole thing rests on a quorum: commitment needs a strict majority, so a five-node cluster tolerates two failures and a three-node cluster tolerates one, which is why Raft clusters are sized at odd numbers.

In practice Raft powers the coordination and metadata planes of major systems. etcd uses Raft to store Kubernetes cluster state so every control-plane component reads the same truth. Consul uses Raft to keep its service catalog and key-value store consistent for service discovery and configuration. Kafka's KRaft mode uses a Raft-based metadata log to replace ZooKeeper, so brokers agree on topic, partition, and leadership metadata without a separate coordination system. The nuance I would stress is that Raft is used for the small, critical, strongly-consistent state — who is the leader, what is the configuration, cluster membership — not for the bulk, high-throughput data plane, because requiring a majority to acknowledge every write would not scale to millions of transactions.

In my banking work this distinction mattered: I would use a Raft-backed store like etcd to agree on something small and critical, such as which data centre is the current primary for transfers or a distributed lock ensuring only one node runs a settlement job, while the actual transaction throughput is handled by the data store that Raft coordinates. The demo I think about is a five-node cluster that elects a leader by majority, commits a primary-selection entry once a majority store it, then loses the leader and re-elects a new one that still has the committed decision — proving that a committed entry survives a leader change and the cluster never produces two conflicting answers. The principle I take into interviews is that Raft gives you a strongly-consistent, fault-tolerant agreed log for the small critical state that must never diverge, and knowing that it belongs in the coordination plane rather than the data plane is what separates genuinely understanding it from merely naming it.
